stories.body:
Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. There is little chance of that

N ot much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.

Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.

The IMF is right when it says countries have shown resilience when having to cope with so many headwinds. It could have been worse. A lot worse. There was even some good news for the UK, with the IMF upgrading its growth forecast for this year and praising the government for its deficit-reduction plan.

The better-than-expected performance of the global economy breaks with historical precedent. In the past, oil shocks of the magnitude witnessed since the start of Iran war have had a marked and immediate impact, but there are three key reasons why growth has remained robust and inflationary pressure has been muted this time.

The first is the massive amount of investment in the development of artificial intelligence. This has been particularly important in the US, which is comfortably the fastest growing member of the G7 group of major developed economies year on year. The second is that countries have drawn on inventories of oil, and that has helped to alleviate the loss of crude from the Middle East. Had stockpiles not been run down, oil prices would have risen even more sharply. The third is that China’s economic strategy relies on exporting cheap goods to the rest of the world, and this is bearing down on the prices of imports elsewhere.

All that said, the potential flashpoints for trouble are everywhere. The situation in the Middle East is deteriorating, with the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia. Oil stocks are running low and Donald Trump has got the US into just the sort of forever war that he used to rail against. The downside to cheap Chinese goods is that they are threatening manufacturing jobs in the west, with Germany especially vulnerable.

Meanwhile, massive US investment in AI has pushed up the cost of borrowing and resulted in shortages of capital for non-AI sectors. Governments are coming under pressure to rein in spending or raise taxes in the hope that bond markets will be impressed by their efforts to cut budget deficits.

Warnings from (among others) the head of the IMF , Kristalina Georgieva, and the governor of the Bank of England , Andrew Bailey, of the need to run a tighter fiscal ship come at a time when voters want politicians to do more, not less. There is little appetite for a new era of austerity, and finance ministers know it. If they follow through on the tough talk and actually deliver painful measures, the backlash is likely to be brutal.

Just as big a problem for governments is the need – at a time when global supply chains are stretched and fragile – to boost national self-sufficiency. The student protests in India and France highlight the pressures on states to intervene. Yet the capacity of states to act effectively is much weaker than they care to admit.

At a time when globalisation is in retreat, there is a need for a strong system of multilateral cooperation to cope with the strains. That is not currently the case. The World Trade Organization is moribund in this new age of protectionism, and the IMF and the World Bank are reluctant to call Trump out for his erratic behaviour.

Yet the idea that a new era of partnership will flower when there is a new US president is for the birds. The problems of multilateralism run far deeper than that. The liberal world order that the IMF and World Bank have presided over since the end of the second world war was dysfunctional long before Trump arrived in office.

As the former UN official Richard Kozul-Wright points out in a paper published next month, the IMF and World Bank – created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference – may still be operational but they have lost their connection to the New Deal principles laid out 82 years ago: state intervention in the running of economies, active industrial policy, the pursuit of full employment and help for poor countries to develop. “Instead, they have in recent decades pursued an agenda which encourages footloose capital, bolsters (and protects) private profit, and reduces the policy space available to governments. As a result, they have acted as hand maidens to an age of rising inequality, debt distress and heightened anxiety.”

after newsletter promotion

The IMF’s own programmes for countries that come looking for financial assistance illustrate Kozul-Wright’s point about the lack of policy space . Help comes with strings attached: an insistence on tax increases and spending cuts that are frontloaded so that half the measures are implemented in the first year and two-thirds within two years.

The IMF argues that this “tough love” has a higher chance of success, although its view of what constitutes success is limited, and primarily means that a borrowing country doesn’t need another IMF programme in the next three years. It doesn’t mean living standards are improving or that fewer people are in poverty.

Clearly it would help to return to New Deal principles. It would mean governments had more policy space to develop strategies tailored to their own needs. It would mean a boost to public investment. It would mean a new Marshall plan to help poorer countries cope with the climate crisis. It would mean a serious attempt to tackle debt distress. But, in all honesty, none of that has a chance of happening any time soon. As a result, the world will become hotter, more fractured, more prone to conflict, less equal and a lot angrier.

The IMF is worried that the limits of this resilience may soon be tested , and it is right to be worried. Peace in the Middle East would bring oil prices tumbling down, but unless that happens quickly a long winter lies ahead. This looks more like a crisis postponed than a crisis permanently avoided. A lull before the storm, in all probability.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

stories.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay. As the petition explains: Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology. We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting. This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following SIREN v. San Jose. Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree. Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition Read the press release Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay

stories.title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
stories.summary: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 October 2026, 14:07 BST

Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.

The culture secretary said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.

Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from Nandy and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.

"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.

The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.

The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the competition watchdog, forcing it to investigate the tie-up.

A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."

stories.title: US producer inflation soars amid gasoline surge; John Healey says UK banks are part of ‘jewel in the crown’ – business live
stories.summary: John Healey has spoken to UK journalists at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok, and said banks are a part of the “jewel” in the UK’s economic crown John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget Today’s better-than-forecast UK growth report is good news for chancellor John Healey as he hobnobs with other finance ministers at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. But it may encourage the Bank of England to raise interest rates as soon as its next meeting in November…. “While August’s unexpected uptick all but confirms that the OBR will raise its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.4%, the Chancellor still faces a major Budget headache, as elevated borrowing costs eat into fiscal headroom and increase pressure for tax rises. “These unexpectedly upbeat figures will further embolden hawkish sentiment among policymakers by reinforcing the view that the economy is strong enough to withstand a rate rise, making a November hike look highly likely.” “The latest GDP figures are encouraging, with the economy growing by 0.7% in the three months to August, its strongest growth rate since May. On its current trajectory, the UK is likely to record growth comfortably above 1% this year, which would probably be enough to make it the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7. “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure. stories.body:
Healey quizzed about bank tax plans

Over at the IMF’s annual meeting in Bangkok today, chancellor John Healey is meeting with UK journalists now, including my colleague Heather Stewart .

Healey , who should be cheered by the news that the UK economy grew unexpectedly in August , was asked whether he plans to impose new taxes on the bank sector, and replies:

double quotation mark “I don’t want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks’ time. My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects. That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time.

Healey added that his “special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future” – echoing what he told Sky News a few minutes ago .

The chancellor also welcomed the IMF’s support for the UK’s fiscal plans.

Today’s jump in wholesale US inflation increases the pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates soon.

Waleed Said , technical analyst at GivTrade , says the increase in core PPI means the energy shock from the Iran war is spreading, adding:

double quotation mark A firmer Fed is more likely but the market pricing about a one in three chance of a hike in October so don’t overreact to the headline but a rate hike in December does seem imminent.

US PPI inflation driven up by soaring gasoline

Tin hats on!

New data from the US has shown that producers are hiking prices at their fastest rate in almost four years, and much faster than expected.

Ths increase was driven by a surge in energy prices, which more than wiped out a drop in egg prices.

The Producer Price Index, which measures how much goods makers and services firms charge for their wares, jumped by 6.3% in the year to September. That’s the largest 12-month increase since December 2022, when it rose by 6.4%.

On a monthly basis, prices climbed by 1.2% in September alone, a sign that inflationary pressures rose last month.

The report shows that goods prices jumped by 2.6% in September alone, the largest increase since data were first calculated in December 2009.

That was driven by the rise in motor fuel; The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports:

double quotation mark Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs dropped 39.7 percent.

Alarmingly, core PPI also jumped. Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0% in the year to September.

PPI is an important measure, as increases in producer prices tend to be passed onto consumers, who already experienced a jump in inflation last month:

EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China

The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc’s vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.

EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for “new instruments to better address these imbalances” according to a draft statement.

The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.

EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.

The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.

Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.

The EU’s two biggest economies are also seeking “a diversification instrument” that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the “kill switch”, the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.

Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise “they are killing their customers” , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.

The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU’s point of view: “We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost.”

UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal

Media news: The UK government is ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s£1.6bn deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm.

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, has told parliament she believes there are public interest grounds for intervening in the deal.

They include ‘the need for free expression of opinion in news media’, the need for a pluratity of views in the news, and the need for a wide range of broadcasting which is “of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests.”

Back in July, Sky said the deal was a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion”.

Labour MPs urge Healey to raise taxes on slot machines

Nearly 90 Labour MPs have urged the Chancellor, John Healey, to ignore the gambling sector’s warnings about job losses and double the tax on high street slot machines at his inaugural budget later this month.

Campaigners say raising “machine games duty” (MGD) from 20% to 40% could raise £460m to fund public services and reduce the harm caused by 24-hour slots venues.

But Healey is also under pressure from the UK’s £13bn-a-year gambling industry, which has warned of up to 16,000 job losses at casinos and bookmakers , if the tax rise goes ahead.

In a letter sent on Thursday, 88 Labour MPs – nearly a quarter of the party’s backbenchers – demanded that “those who profit most from products associated with the greatest harm should be taxed at a higher rate”.

Their main target is “Category B3” slot machines, which allow punters to place rapid fire stakes of £2 every 2.5 seconds, for a chance of a £500 jackpot. Fruit machines in pubs, which are usually Category C, should be exempt, they said.

There were 49,094 B3 machines in Great Britain as of June 2024, racking up annual takings of nearly £2bn according to Gambling Commission figures. Each terminal took an average of £40,127 during that year, more than the median UK salary.

The MPs cited evidence from the regulator that players of these machines are “among the groups most likely to contact gambling help services, that those with gambling problems play gaming machines more frequently than those with fewer problems, and that problem gamblers spend relatively more time and money on machines.”

The Guardian has previously exposed how so-called adult gaming centres (AGCs), known by some in the industry as “slot farms” have exploited vulnerable gamblers and taken advantage of lax planning laws to flood high streets with the machines in the UK’s poorest areas .

The machines “depend on repeated local losses, often in communities least able to afford them” according to the letter, led by Alex Ballinger MP.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is understood to be supportive of measures that would crack down on AGCs, having been a vocal critic of them as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

Earlier this week the bosses of firms including Ladbrokes and Paddy Power signed a last-ditch letter to Healey, predicting that doubling MGD could trigger up to 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casino closures and 15,900 job losses.

Signatories included Britain’s largest taxpayer, Fred Done, whose family have earned £105m in dividends from their gambling business since 2022.

UK consumers’ pre-Christmas spending to rise, partly thanks to inflation

The UK economy could get a festive boost from a jump in spending this Christmas, new research shows.

Bain & Company are forecasting that UK consumers’ spending will register the strongest rise in 4 years in the pre-Christmas season this year. Nominal sales are projected to grow 3.5% in the November-December trading period, compared to the same period last year.

However, about half that increase is due to inflation! Higher price mean consumers are forced to pay more at the till for their Christmas shopping, even before adding more to this year’s Christmas stockings.

Sales volumes could grow in clothing & accessories, electronics & appliances, and health & personal care products, Bain suggests.

The group adds:

double quotation mark The Bain Consumer Lab findings also show UK consumers expect to do more of their shopping online this Christmas season. 42% of survey respondents said they plan to do all or most online vs 18% who plan to do all or most in-store. Of online shoppers, 69% say they will start their shopping journey on Amazon while 20% say they will start their shopping on AI platforms.

Toy shop Hamleys reported this week that a cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” will be among the top Christmas presents this year….so lets hope John Healey leaves us with enough money for one of those!

US tech stocks are expected to fall when trading begins in under two and a half hour’s time.

The futures market indicates the Nasdaq index could drop by around 1.2%, adding to yesterday’s fall of almost 1.9%.

Charu Chanana , chief investment strategist at Saxo says the markets are getting increasingly nervous, despite strong results from tech companies such as ASML and Micron, adding:

double quotation mark AI demand is not the problem; expectations and financing are. CoreWeave’s bond selloff highlights growing scrutiny of debt-funded AI infrastructure and the cost of capital.

The IMF warned today that the Middle East region is suffering a highly uneven economic shock this year.

Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the Fund pointed out.

Jihad Azour , the IMF’s director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told a news conference:

double quotation mark “The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability.”

Back in the financial markets, US government borrowing costs are heading for their biggest daily drop in over a year.

The sell-off in AI-linked stocks, such as chipmakers, today is driving investors into bonds instead. And the US, as well as the UK, is benefitting.

Ten-year US Treasury yields are down 11 basis points today to 5.08%, which Reuters has spotted would be the largest one-day decline since early August 2025.

Elsewhere in Bangkok today, Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden has said UK firms are trying to cut custs in response to the energy price shock, rather than just lift their prices.

That trend should make it easier for the central bank to contain inflation, and limit pressure to raise interest rates.

Speaking to CNBC TV on the sidelines of the IMF’s annual meeting, Breedon said:

double quotation mark “What’s really different now, relative to when we had the last energy shock in 2022, is that people aren’t looking to push costs through. “There’s a desire to absorb the shock rather than just pass it on, which makes our job as monetary policymakers a bit easier in these uncertain times.”

Healey: Banks are part of 'jewel in the crown' of UK economy

Intriguingly, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey has told Bloomberg that banks are a part of the “jewel” in the UK’s economic crown.

That, alongside his comments to UK journalists in Bangkok that banks are “hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects” could, perhaps, dampen speculation that the budget might contain a bank tax.

Healey told Bloomberg :

double quotation mark “They’re a big contributor to the economy… “They [the banks] are a part of the jewel, if you like, in the British economic crown.”

Important to note that Healey was very keen to avoid pre-budget speculation this morning, pointing out how economically damaging it could be .

Last week, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) calculated that tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues.

The TUC argues that the government should reverse the cut to the bank surcharge made in 2023 by Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk.

Healey working on more support for Ukraine

John Healey wrapped up his meeting with the UK press pack in Bangkok with a heavy hint that he is preparing to offer more support to Ukraine at the budget.

Healey , who was of course defence secretary earlier this year, said:

double quotation mark “Now is the time to step up pressure on Putin and step up support for Ukraine.”

Asked if that could come as soon as the budget, Healey said:

double quotation mark “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine, military, diplomatic, and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with Putin targeting these energy systems , leaving thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching. The future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”

Healey pledges to stick to fiscal rules

The press pack are now pressing John Healey on whether he will stick to the UK’s fiscal rules (which were a big part of his predecessor Rachel Reeves).

Healey pledges to meet those rules (that day-to-day public spending must be covered by tax revenues, and that debt is falling as a share of GDP by the 2029/30 financial year).

Healey tells reporters in Bangkok:

double quotation mark “The test year is now just three years ahead, so this is a tighter set of fiscal rules than we had before. It’s not five years out, four years out - it’s in three years, 2029-2030, with borrowing set to fall and current spending covered by what we raise. We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.”

Healey: Closer UK-EU links are important

Asked about the potential economic benefits for the UK of potentially rejoining the European Union, John Healey said:

double quotation mark “Those sort of matters may become part of a wider conversation that the prime minister’s keen to keen to encourage, because his basic starting point is one that very few people would dispute - that Brexit has not been good for for Britain. But my task now, whatever happens in the future, is to make sure that we do our best to open up access to the markets where we can. That’s what the European Summit is designed to do in specific areas. You know, we’ve got a big argument with Europe over the way that they frame their Made in Europe plans, just as we have over access to some of their defence. And that big argument is, at this time of all times, when you have a strengthening US, a more resurgent China, actually, the strength of Europe beyond the European Union is enhanced in the economy and the national security side. If other European nations like us, like Norway, have contributions to make, we can do so with them.”

Reminder: earlier this week, Andy Burnham said the existing UK-EU relationship is “not good enough”.

The UK is also lobbying hard to be included in the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation , amid fears of the damage if British manufacturers are locked out.

stories.title: Labour could end local coalitions with Greens over Zionism policy
stories.summary: Labour says it will end power-sharing deals with councillors that do not disown the party's new stance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sheffield is one of the areas where Labour currently shares power with the Greens

Published 46 minutes ago

Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Green Party on local councils, unless its councillors disown the party's newly-adopted policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

Labour says it will give local Green groups seven days to confirm they reject the policy, which was recently approved by Green members at its party conference.

Labour says its ultimatum applies to 19 councils where it shares power with the Greens, either directly or alongside other parties.

The Greens hit back at the move, accusing Labour of meddling and arguing it would be undemocratic for the party to "tell local parties what to do".

The policy motion adopted by members of the Green Party of England and Wales said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.

It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has led to a backlash from Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including four of its five MPs.

Green leader Zack Polanski, who skipped the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, has said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.

He has however said that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology", arguing this was the "substantial part" of the motion. Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.

Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In other areas, it runs the council as part of a broader coalition alongside other parties.

Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion Published 20 hours ago

Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote Published 5 October

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy, although Downing Street did not confirm what this meant for local government.

The party has now said it wants all local Labour groups to write to their Green counterparts, demanding "clear and unambiguous" statements rejecting the policy.

Green groups will also be asked to call on their party's "national leadership" to reconsider the policy.

"Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end," the party's chair Bridget Phillipson said.

In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong.

"Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic".

National parties exercise various levels of control over groups of local councillors who wish to do deals to govern locally.

Labour councillors require the approval of its ruling National Executive Committee before entering into local tie-ups.

According to the party's rulebook, local groups must also "stand down" from power sharing arrangements when asked to do so by their regional office.

By contrast, the Green Party of England and Wales allows local groups to make the final decision on where and whether to share power locally.

stories.title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
stories.summary: EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post. The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process. TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “ committed to protecting traveler privacy ,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case. The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.” The OIG further admonished the agency: TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed. We hope the TSA will fix these issues. The OIG summary states: We issued one finding and three recommendations to strengthen controls, improve oversight, and ensure transparency and the proper handling of passenger data. TSA concurred with all three recommendations. Two recommendations are open and resolved, and one remains open and unresolved. Why EFF Opposes the Government’s Use of Facial Recognition Technology EFF has a long history of opposing governmental use of facial recognition technology. EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post.

The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process.

TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “ committed to protecting traveler privacy ,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case.

The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.”

The OIG further admonished the agency:

TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed.

We hope the TSA will fix these issues. The OIG summary states:

We issued one finding and three recommendations to strengthen controls, improve oversight, and ensure transparency and the proper handling of passenger data. TSA concurred with all three recommendations. Two recommendations are open and resolved, and one remains open and unresolved.

Why EFF Opposes the Government’s Use of Facial Recognition Technology

EFF has a long history of opposing governmental use of facial recognition technology. As the OIG’s audit underscores, this technology presents privacy risks associated with unsecured data, unauthorized access, and data breaches. The government’s use of this technology also creates a mass surveillance system and facilitates the creation of warrantless biometric records for unconsenting parties.

The biometric data captured by this technology is not without errors. There have been multiple instances of law enforcement agencies using facial recognition technology to misidentify and arrest innocent individuals.

Reminder: Opting Out of TSA Photos Is Possible

Given that facial recognition technology is prone to mistakes, combined with the OIG’s audit revealing significant privacy weaknesses, it is imperative that travelers remember that opting out is possible. TSA’s own website emphasizes that travelers who wish to decline to have their photo taken for facial comparison can do so without any delay, disruption, or recourse.

Considering the data protection weaknesses exposed by the OIG’s audit, EFF will continue to oppose this governmental system of mass surveillance and spread awareness to ensure that no one is forced to relinquish their biometric data without consent.

stories.title: Trump commercial railing against his enemies kept airing after court blocked it
stories.summary: US attorney apologized to court, said government has stopped running Trump ads.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US attorney apologized to court, said government has stopped running Trump ads.

Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda.

In the most widely aired commercial, Trump railed against his perceived enemies and said he would “liberate America from these villains once and for all.” The campaign also included a commercial praising Trump’s record as president, another in which Trump calls the US the “most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history,” and commercials related to the Iran war and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. The order said the government must cancel the ads, “including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026.”

The Trump administration had told the court on October 10 that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertising purchases were set to expire on October 11 and would not be renewed. Despite that, the ads continued airing the night of October 11 and on part of October 12. This was also a week after Trump’s October 5 statement that he would start paying for the ads “myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

A US attorney yesterday filed a status report saying that the government is now complying with the order and issued an apology. “As Your Honor is aware, the Court emailed the TRO to the parties yesterday at 6:46 p.m.,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald wrote in a filing . “Counsel for the Government emailed the TRO to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m. Agency counsel did not become aware of Government counsel’s email until this morning. The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs.”

The ads aired as part of a $20 million purchase order that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) made on September 20 with LMD Agency, an ad firm. The DHS told the court that the ad placements through October 11 cost $19 million.

Trump admin said ads would stop Sunday

In the previous Trump administration filing opposing the motion for a temporary restraining order, one of the government’s arguments was that a court order was unnecessary because the ads would not run past October 11. It said:

DHS issued a purchase order to obtain media services from a vendor in support of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for placing national media buys. The vendor has currently purchased media buys under the terms of the purchase order through tomorrow, October 11, 2026. DHS has directed the vendor not to make any additional media buys past October 11, and DHS has no plans to make any additional media buys under the purchase order or otherwise use appropriated funds on any similar contracts for the creation or distribution of the media that is the subject of this lawsuit. Accordingly, the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow, and Plaintiffs therefore will suffer no harm, let alone irreparable harm, absent an injunction.

The Washington Post reported yesterday that the ads kept running after the restraining order took effect. Nonprofit advocacy group Common Cause and other groups that sued the government submitted a filing later in the day notifying the court of the government’s noncompliance.

The Trump ads continued airing on programs including 60 Minutes , ABC World News Tonight , and America’s Funniest Home Videos . They ran nearly 400 times after the restraining order took effect, including 32 times on Monday, according to AdImpact data cited in the plaintiffs’ court filing.

“Plaintiffs do not presently seek contempt sanctions,” the groups said. “But given that the ads have continued to run on October 12—the day after Defendants insisted the ad-buy was no longer effective—Plaintiffs request a status conference to determine Defendants’ compliance.”

Judge: Ads “are purely partisan”

After the government filed its status report, Rochon scheduled a hearing for Wednesday “to discuss this and next steps in this action.” The lawsuit is in US District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The plaintiffs are Common Cause; Robert Hunter, a Democratic candidate for a state legislature seat in Alabama; Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ; and Empire State 32BJ SEIU PAC. Defendants include DHS, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the Executive Office of the President.

Rochon found that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their claim that the Trump administration violated the 2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act requirement that no funding may be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

“Defendants do not contest that the at-issue advertisements are purely partisan and unconnected to DHS’s official functions,” Rochon wrote. “Thus, the Court finds that Moving Plaintiffs are likely to succeed in showing that the advertisements are impermissible ‘publicity or propaganda’ under Section 718 [of the Consolidated Appropriations Act].”

Trump recycled ad from 2024 campaign

One of the ads “is almost identical to one used during President Trump’s 2024 campaign, other than the fact that its funding disclaimer now identifies the United States government rather than his presidential campaign,” Rochon wrote. “It depicts President Trump walking down a hallway while delivering a series of statements about his political adversaries. Among other things, he promises to ‘demolish the deep state,’ ‘drive out the globalists,’ ‘cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,’ ‘throw off the sick political class that hates our country,’ and ‘rout the fake news media.’ This advertisement provides no information about DHS’s official functions.”

As of October 8, the ad “had aired approximately 9,679 times, generating an estimated 972 million impressions at an estimated cost exceeding $9.09 million,” Rochon wrote. Another $6.3 million was estimated to have been spent on four other government-funded ads challenged in the lawsuit. That’s about $15.4 million as of October 8, and more was spent over the next few days.

Rochon found “a clear and substantial likelihood” that the Trump administration violated the Administrative Procedure Act “because Congress did not appropriate funds for DHS to spend on disseminating the challenged advertisements.” Rochon said a restraining order was necessary despite the DHS claim that it had “no plans” to continue running the ads.

“Defendants also have not provided reasonable assurances that OMB will not reapportion funds from another source to continue running similar advertisements,” she wrote.

The temporary restraining order is in place for only two weeks, but it can be converted into a preliminary injunction that would keep the ads off the air while litigation continues. Trump, the White House, OMB, and DHS face a similar lawsuit filed by the Democratic National Committee in the federal court in the District of Columbia. A hearing on a motion for a temporary restraining order in that case is scheduled for Thursday.

Watch: Reform UK councillor filmed making racist comments, ITV investigation shows

Published 14 October 2026

Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform, , external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

It comes after Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to root out "bad apples" from his party.

A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.

The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.

ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform – the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.

He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than 1% of British population can be non-white."

On a different day, Feeney, Solihull's deputy mayor, is joined by two other Reform candidates, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, who discuss speculation of a mosque being built in the local area.

"There's got to be a way of stopping them - like, go and buy some pork chops; we'll bury it in the ground," Campbell is heard saying in the film.

Whelan says "we'll take pictures of it", prompting Feeney to add: "I was gonna say, 'Unfortunately, this is a pig cemetery, mate'."

Discussing a female Reform candidate from Birmingham, Feeney is heard saying, "I didn't know where to look," before Whelan adds: "I'd have been sniffing that seat as soon as she got up."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons" and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

ITV reported that Whelan, who did not respond to the broadcaster's request for comment, would now be an independent councillor. The BBC has contacted him and Campbell for a response.

Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples".

Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".

"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.

Elsewhere in the film, Dean Miller, a councillor in the south London borough of Bromley, is shown campaigning for Reform in the Makerfield by-election.

"We've been ethnically cleansed out of London because you never used to get any blacks over in Bromley," he tells an ITV undercover reporter. "And now, you know, Bromley's like massive Nigerian communities there."

Miller says he is "not racist", before later adding: "The Muslim thing, that is going to be that thing that takes over everything and then everyone just has one religion. Because, apparently, King Charles is a [expletive] Muslim... I think that's [expletive] traitorous."

ITV reported that Miller would now sit as an independent councillor having resigned from Reform and had told them in a statement that he was heavily medicated due to a chronic pain condition when he made the comments.

The BBC has contacted him for comment.

In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."

The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

International alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship

The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.

An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.

“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.

The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.

It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.

Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem.

Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform.

Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.

A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”.

“We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added.

The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”.

The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added.

While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.

The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.

Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities.

after newsletter promotion

The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.

“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.

The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests.

But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”.

It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.

However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.

“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.

“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll

Our reporters answer your questions about the US economy and the midterm elections

With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.

The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.

The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.

Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy is worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.

Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy is getting better.

Voters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs.

Recent inflation data showed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990.

Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according to AAA .

Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in the video .

“They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul el-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan, said at a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there is an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.

Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.

Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party has a solution compared with Democrats (17%)

Half of independents said neither party has a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.

Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared to their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they are living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans.

When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations.

This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 U S adults.

stories.title: How a Chinese-made toy gets to a US retailer
stories.summary: With Christmas on the horizon, we trace children's toys from factories in China to US shelves.

stories.body:
China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US

Published 15 October 2026, 00:01 BST

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

The factory

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

The ship

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

The US border

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The US toy company

Jay Foreman says that most of the money spent on a toy in the US doesn't leave the country

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Getting a toy onto the shelves in the US requires both a lot of work and a long journey.
