stories.title: Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency.
stories.summary: The post Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A photo collage featuring a portrait of Texas Governor Greg Abbott surrounded by official state seal stamps, date stamps, border wall imagery, and clips of text declaring a state of disaster.
stories.body:
Since Texas Gov. Greg Abbott first declared an emergency at the border in 2021, he’s renewed or amended the proclamation at least 69 times. The proclamation has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state Legislature.

Co-published with The Texas Tribune

Last month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott repeated a claim he’s made for the past five years. He stated that the number of people crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally “posed an ongoing and imminent threat” across the state. In doing so, he renewed a border security disaster proclamation that has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state Legislature.

Abbott’s declaration stands in sharp contrast to the numbers reported by the Trump administration, which says the drop in the flow of migrants crossing the border has been unprecedented and has reached historic lows since it took over in January 2025.

Yet, since Abbott first declared an emergency at the border during the Biden administration in 2021, he’s renewed or amended the proclamation at least 69 times — 21 of those during Trump’s tenure.

The Republican governor, who is running for his fourth term next month, has consolidated power like no Texas governor before him, building on his predecessors’ efforts to strengthen what by design is supposed to be a “weak governor” state as the constitution limits what can be done without legislative approval, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune have reported. One of the methods he’s used to do that is issuing executive orders and disaster declarations that allow him to shift funds, suspend regulations and award no-bid contracts at times of emergency.

Since January 2025, two of the top agencies involved with border enforcement — the Department of Public Safety and the Texas Military Department — have awarded more than $5 million in noncompetitive contracts citing the emergency for items like a Ford F-150, rifles and apartments, state records show.

“I think it’s unprecedented,” said Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas. “I don’t think that there is a similar example, certainly not as to the length of the emergency, and certainly not after the emergency has seemed to pass.”

Abbott’s office did not respond to specific questions for this story, including about the noncompetitive contracts, but Deputy Press Secretary Madeline Waschak said in a written statement that the governor has been clear that border security is an ongoing priority.

“The damage caused by four years of failed border policies under Democrat rule did not disappear overnight, and the progress we have made will not sustain itself without continued vigilance,” she wrote.

“Securing the border requires constant, deliberate action to combat illegal crossings, cartel smuggling, fentanyl trafficking, and other criminal activity that threatens public safety in Texas. Governor Abbott will ensure the tools remain in place to safeguard our state as we work alongside the Trump Administration to deter, arrest, detain, and deport illegal immigrants,” she added.

At the time of Abbott’s first border declaration, four months into President Joe Biden’s term, Border Patrol was making more than 180,000 apprehensions along the southwest border in a single month. According to Abbott, the federal government’s inability or unwillingness to enforce immigration laws had created a humanitarian crisis in many communities in Texas.

“The Biden Administration’s open-border policies have enabled escalating violence from the cartels, dramatically increased the risk of human trafficking, and created a severe crisis of illegal drugs crossing into the United States,” the order stated .

Since then, apprehensions along the southwest border have dropped on average to about 8,000 a month this year.

The border security declaration remains Abbott’s longest continuously running emergency proclamation. Abbott similarly renewed his 2020 COVID-19 disaster declaration for three years, even as he downplayed the severity of the pandemic.

“This is the quiet power of the governor,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston. “It’s not something often that they brag about because the more that it becomes a political issue, the more that there might be some contestation of it.”

Other than border security, the governor’s second longest-running emergency declaration is related to droughts. He declared a state disaster in July 2022 and within days amended it bringing the total of counties to 189. He’s continued to renew it, but now it applies to about a third of the counties originally identified.

State lawmakers have repeatedly tried — and failed — to curb the governor’s powers under the state’s disaster act. Last year, legislators from both parties filed at least a handful of measures that would mandate Abbott get approval from the Legislature if he wanted to extend a disaster declaration, but none passed.

Abbott’s emergency declarations have been accompanied by record spending on border security efforts. Texas budgeted over $11 billion during the Biden administration and allotted an additional $3 billion last year, after Trump took office.

It’s all part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, an initiative he launched in March 2021 contending it was needed to stem the smuggling of drugs and people into the country through Texas. Because of the emergency declaration, police could charge immigrants with criminal trespassing for crossing the border through private property, and the governor was able to shift money from other agencies to fund the operation and build border barriers, deploy the National Guard and get help from other states.

Much of the funding for Operation Lone Star is funneled through the Texas Military Department and DPS, two of the agencies responsible for major enforcement efforts. But the governor’s share of border spending has also ballooned since Abbott took office over a decade ago. State lawmakers allotted his office nearly $230 million last year to distribute through grants, largely to local prosecutors and government agencies helping the state with Operation Lone Star.

Though the situation on the ground has changed, one aspect of the emergency declaration has remained constant: the ability of state agencies to award noncompetitive contracts.

DPS and the Texas Military Department have awarded at least six noncompetitive contracts so far during the second Trump administration for work related to the operation where they cite an emergency. This includes a more than $2 million contract to Texas-based CTC Gunworks LLC for rifles and pistols for active-duty personnel. CTC Gunworks officials could not be reached for comment.

Officials with the Texas Military Department referred questions about its procurement process to the governor’s office. A DPS spokesperson said in a written statement that even though the disaster declaration allows for expedited purchases, the department still follows best practices and “aims to select vendors offering the best value, determined by cost, quality, and ability to meet the specific disaster response requirements.”

Regarding the specific contracts, the DPS spokesperson said they were purchases tied to existing state contracts.

The continued funding and expansion of Operation Lone Star has come even as it’s been plagued with problems. In 2022, an investigation by ProPublica, the Tribune and The Marshall Project found that the state’s reported success included arrests unrelated to the border or immigration and counted drug seizures made by troopers from across the state who were not directly assigned to the operation. The Tribune and Army Times also exposed poor working conditions, pay delays and suicides among National Guard members deployed as part of Operation Lone Star.

During a Tribune-hosted event this week with state lawmakers from El Paso, Democratic state Rep. Mary González , vice chair of the Appropriations Committee, said state legislators have already started to scale back when it comes to border funding and there’s interest from both sides of the aisle to continue to do so in the upcoming legislative session.

“I think that the problem is that some of that border security money still lies in the governor’s office which has no checks and balances and because we are still under an emergency — which is not an emergency anymore — an emergency border security statement which he can just use that money, you have seen some questionable appropriations under the veil of border security,” she said.

Abbott, however, has repeatedly said that Texas’ work in securing the border is not over.

“We must secure the border not just for the next two years of the Trump administration, but we gotta do it forever,” Abbott said at a press conference in early October where he discussed the federal government’s $7.5 billion reimbursement for border security expenses the state had incurred.

Rottinghaus said that Texas will always have to confront border crossings and drug trafficking, but the existence of those problems don’t always justify an emergency declaration.

“Even someone who strongly supports the governor’s board of policies might ask whether they want a future governor of the opposite party using the same interpretation of emergency authority for years,” Rottinghaus said, adding that the issue is that “governors, once they get a power, are hesitant to give it back.”

stories.title: Frustrated by Losses in the Courts, Missouri Republicans Want to Change How Top Judges Are Selected
stories.summary: The post Frustrated by Losses in the Courts, Missouri Republicans Want to Change How Top Judges Are Selected appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A man wearing a red sports coat walks through a room of people in suits in a government building.
stories.body:
For 86 years, Missouri has held on to a nonpartisan system of selecting its top judges. But after the state Supreme Court overruled the GOP’s redistricting push, some Republican lawmakers are calling for the system to be overturned.

Some 86 years ago, Missouri voters enshrined a system for selecting top judges that would remove political influence from the courts. And almost immediately, it came under attack.

Under what has come to be known as the Missouri Plan, lawyers help choose a slate of three candidates from which the governor must make an appointment for the state Supreme Court, appeals courts and, in some populous areas, the circuit courts.

In the first years after adoption, it faced pushback from party bosses who had historically used judicial seats for political patronage. They said it gave too much power to the lawyers. Voters, though, decisively defeated a repeal measure in 1942.

More recently, the conservative activist Leonard Leo, who viewed Missouri as a crucial battleground, tried in 2007 to persuade Republican Gov. Matt Blunt to reject a slate of Supreme Court candidates — part of a broader effort to weaken a judicial selection system that had become a model for some two dozen states around the country.

Blunt resisted and picked one of the three judges from the approved slate.

Then, in 2012, GOP lawmakers put a proposed overhaul before voters that, if approved, would have given the governor more control. Voters, by a 3-to-1 margin, turned back the plan.

Now the attacks are back, driven by a new grievance.

At President Donald Trump’s behest, Republican lawmakers redrew the state’s congressional map in a mid-decade gerrymander. The goal: to give the GOP a shot at winning seven of Missouri’s congressional seats, instead of the six it now holds.

But voters gathered enough signatures to force a referendum on the map and put it on hold. While Secretary of State Denny Hoskins tried to keep the referendum off the ballot, the Missouri Supreme Court overruled him. It ordered the old map restored until voters decide on the new one.

Hoskins, citing a federal court ruling that contradicted the state’s highest court, directed officials to use the new map anyway, prompting Chief Justice Brent Powell to demand that Hoskins appear in court to show why he shouldn’t be held in contempt.

Fourteen Republican lawmakers responded by threatening to impeach “responsible members of this Court” for “willful neglect of duty, incompetency and misconduct” if the justices held Hoskins in contempt; the court did so anyway. Hoskins backed down and instructed local election officials to distribute ballots using the old map; the justices decided not to have him arrested.

The drama played out as Republicans in Missouri and elected officials nationwide have sought to weaken institutions that limit their power. In North Carolina, the Republican-dominated General Assembly stripped authority from Democratic governors . In Wisconsin, Republicans threatened to impeach a newly elected Supreme Court justice to protect gerrymandered maps . And in New York, Democrats bypassed an independent commission to pass a gerrymander that favored them, but the state’s highest court struck it down.

Rather than electing top judges, as Illinois does, or giving the governor primary responsibility for choosing them, like California, Missouri selects its appellate and Supreme Court judges through a commission made up of three lawyers, one elected by lawyers in each appellate district; three non-lawyers appointed by the governor, one from each district; and a state Supreme Court judge selected by the court. After they are appointed, judges face a retention vote at the first general election after completing one year in office, then every 12 years, with voters deciding whether they keep their positions.

In response to the controversy, a number of Missouri Republicans have attacked the system. U.S. Rep. Jason Smith called for the state to switch to electing its Supreme Court judges. Republican Party executive director Miles Ross declared on X, “ The Missouri Plan is done .” Dan Seitz, chief of staff to Sen. Brad Hudson, called for replacing it with a system in which the governor could nominate judges directly, subject to Senate confirmation.

State Rep. Cathy Jo Loy, a Carthage Republican who has introduced legislation in each of the past two sessions to replace the Missouri Plan with gubernatorial appointment and Senate confirmation, said she intends to file a new proposal Dec. 1, the first day lawmakers can file bills for next year’s session. Loy said her opposition to the system predates the recent clashes with the Supreme Court. But she acknowledged that those defeats could give the proposal new momentum.

“There will probably be more appetite because there are several senators that feel the same way,” she said.

Republicans, who hold every statewide elected office, supermajorities in both chambers of the legislature and six of the state’s eight congressional seats, seem to have suddenly found the limits of their power . At the ballot box, voters have overwhelmingly rejected major pieces of the party’s agenda, including an effort to weaken their power to bypass the legislature by amending the constitution or putting laws passed by lawmakers to a statewide vote.

Time and again, when elected officials have sought to limit voters’ use of the ballot initiative, the courts have protected voters’ use of direct democracy. Courts repeatedly rewrote ballot summaries prepared by Republican state officials that they found unfair or misleading, including language describing the initiative that ultimately established abortion rights in 2024.

By the end of that year, after the Missouri Supreme Court rejected a last-minute effort by Republican lawmakers and anti-abortion activists to keep the abortion measure off the ballot, Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin was calling to repeal the Missouri Plan. She proposed replacing the system for selecting Supreme Court and appellate judges with a nonpartisan election. But her bill stalled in committee.

Then came Hoskins. The former state representative and senator from west-central Missouri took office as secretary of state in January 2025 and brought a more combative approach to overseeing elections and ballot measures. Hoskins made a bright-red sport coat his sartorial trademark, often posing with a wood baseball bat and speaking about politics as a series of battles and himself as a conservative warrior.

Hoskins didn’t respond to questions sent to his office. He has previously said that he disagreed with any suggestion that he and Republican leaders were defying the will of voters . He hasn’t publicly called for changing how Missouri selects Supreme Court judges, but his office’s official X social media account reposted Smith’s message calling for the end of the Missouri Plan.

Gov. Mike Kehoe also complained, saying in a post on X that “unelected judges” have shown a “lack of respect for the legislative process.” On a radio show the next day, Kehoe acknowledged that changing how judges are selected hadn’t even been on his radar before the ruling.

“But I think it’s definitely something a lot of people are going to start asking about,” he said. “And I’m not sure the judges across our state, whether Supreme Court or other judges, really wanted that on people’s radar screen.”

Kehoe’s office said it would not respond to questions from ProPublica.

Although some Republicans have derided the state Supreme Court as being a bastion of liberal activists, five of the Supreme Court’s seven judges were appointed by Republican governors. Among them is Powell, whom the then-chair of the state GOP hailed as a “good conservative” before Republican Gov. Eric Greitens selected him in 2017.

Powell, who also serves as chair of the judicial selection commission, declined to comment for this story. In remarks on Sept. 17 to the joint annual meeting of the Missouri Bar and the Judicial Conference of Missouri, he warned of “threats from those who seek to detract from the ideals of our republic and to undermine faith in our sacred institutions — including our legal profession and our courts.”

“It is incumbent on all of us as lawyers and judges to rise up and defend our constitutions and the rule of law,” he added.

Whether there’s enough support to repeal the Missouri Plan remains to be seen. Peverill Squire, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Missouri, said some of the bills that would eliminate the Missouri Plan might go to committee hearings, “but my guess is there probably won’t be enough appetite among enough Republicans to really want to put it on the ballot.”

Any change would ultimately have to be approved by the voters, something Loy acknowledged could be difficult after Republicans’ recent losses at the ballot box.

But the renewed calls have also mobilized the system’s longtime defenders. Ed Dowd, a former U.S. attorney who for two decades has helped lead the Citizens for Missouri Courts, a campaign that advocates for preserving the Missouri Plan, said the group has historically become most active when the system is under threat.

Dowd’s St. Louis-based firm, Dowd Bennett, recently contributed $100,000 to the campaign.

“It’s something that we take very, very seriously and don’t want to take any chances on losing something that we have that works so well,” he said.

stories.body:
Le 24 septembre 2026, le Mali a lancé la phase opérationnelle de sa Stratégie nationale de lutte contre la mendicité .

Nos recherches éclairent une question complémentaire : qui sont ces enfants, et comment se retrouvent-ils à la rue ? Des enfants réunis sur un même trottoir n'y sont pas arrivés de la même manière, et n'appellent pas la même réponse.

J'ai étudié l’enfance , les systèmes familiaux et la protection de l’enfance au Mali et en Afrique de l’Ouest. Dans cet article, j'apporte quelques éléments de réponse.

Une enquête ethnographique

La Stratégie nationale de lutte contre la mendicité repose sur quatre axes :

les alternatives socio-économiques et la réinsertion des personnes vulnérables;

le renforcement de la responsabilité parentale;

l'encadrement et l'accompagnement des écoles coraniques;

l'intégration progressive de l'enseignement religieux dans le système éducatif national.

Notre recherche de terrain, Confiage et enfants de la rue au Mali , menée de 2017 à 2025 à Bamako et dans des villages de Ségou et de Tombouctou, repose sur des entretiens et des observations auprès d'enfants et de familles , de services publics , d'ONG et d'autorités traditionnelles .

Cette étude qualitative , sans chiffres nationaux, montre d'abord que la grande majorité des enfants des rues ne sont pas abandonnés : ils ont un foyer où revenir le soir.

Une partie seulement, sans foyer, vit jour et nuit dehors, comme je l'ai montré dans un article publié . L'enfant visible en plein jour n'est donc pas forcément celui qui reste quand la ville s'endort. Or, on ne protège pas de la même façon un enfant qui retrouve un adulte chaque soir et un enfant sans contact avec sa famille.

Le confiage : une solidarité sans statut

Ces enfants sont souvent issus d'un confiage : l'enfant appartient à toute sa parenté, qui peut le confier à un proche installé en ville, le plus souvent en raison de la faiblesse des revenus. Le droit ne le reconnait pas : le Code des personnes et de la famille de 2011 ne connaît, pour un enfant dont les parents sont connus et qui vit chez un tiers, que la tutelle et l'adoption-protection.

Les textes encadrant la mobilité des enfants existent, mais leur violation n'est pas sanctionnée . Ces dispositions légales sont d'ailleurs mal connues : le Comité des droits de l'enfant de l'ONU s'en inquiétait dès 1999, et le Mali le reconnaissait déjà dans son rapport de 2005 .

Six parcours, six façons d'arriver dans la rue

Derrière la présence des enfants et des femmes dans la rue se cachent des réalités différentes, entre confiage, survie économique, exploitation et fuite des violences.

Les enfants talibés, confiés par leur père à un marabout du même village, passent la journée à chercher de la nourriture et de l'argent autour des marchés, des gares routières et des feux de signalisation.

Les travailleurs ambulants isolés, souvent non scolarisés et loin de leur famille d'origine, vendent de petits services toute l'année.

Les filles aides-ménagères, envoyées dès 12 ans en ville, travaillent en maison. Leur départ est parfois encouragé par leurs mères. Leur salaire, aléatoire, varie de 10 000 à 20 000 francs CFA par mois (17 à 34 dollars américains par mois). Elles travaillent de quatre heures du matin à minuit, sans congé ni week-end. Le Code du travail , pourtant applicable aux particuliers, exige douze heures de repos pour les enfants, un repos hebdomadaire de vingt-quatre heures, et interdit en principe l'emploi avant quinze ans.

Des intermédiaires et des employeurs gardent parfois leurs salaires, sous de fausses accusations de vol.

Les enfants assistants de personnes dépendantes accompagnent une personne âgée ou handicapée dans la mendicité.

Les femmes qui mendient avec de très jeunes enfants, parfois présentés comme jumeaux, cherchent dans la rue, selon leur récit, de quoi subsister, en raison d'une extrême pauvreté.

Les enfants qui ont fui des punitions ou un confiage maltraitant dorment dehors et évitent leur famille par crainte d'être renvoyés.

Ces parcours partagent la rue, l'extrême pauvreté et surtout la mendicité, mais appellent des réponses différentes.

Une histoire de village, de marabout et de ration

Un garçon de 13 ans m'a confié :

C'est mon père qui m'a amené chez le marabout. Il est reparti au village, et ma maman n'était pas d'accord.

Sans revenus stables, le marabout accueille de nombreux enfants que leurs parents nourrissent à peine.

Les enfants vont chercher leur ration auprès de la population, pratique héritée d'un contexte traditionnel dépassé, qui les expose à des dérives que la loi ne tolère pas. L'absence d'encadrement de ces écoles par l'État a contribué à leur mendicité.

Agir en trois étages

Pour lutter durablement contre la présence des enfants dans la rue, il faut agir à la source des départs, mieux encadrer les pratiques qui exposent les mineurs à l’exploitation et préparer leur retour dans des conditions qui empêchent une nouvelle rupture.

Il faut cartographier les parcours, pas seulement les lieux où l'on rencontre les enfants, et agir dans les régions de départ comme Sikasso, Ségou, Tombouctou et Mopti.

À l’avenir, les enfants doivent être maintenus au village, grâce à un soutien aux revenus, à l’école et à l’enseignement coranique de proximité.

Au Niger, une étude de 2022 propose des activités génératrices de revenus et des cantines scolaires

Donner un cadre à ce qui n'en a pas

Il faut conditionner l’agrément des écoles coraniques à leur inscription dans un registre, à l’accréditation des maîtres et à un enseignement de proximité, d’abord pour les nouvelles ouvertures, puis progressivement pour les écoles existantes. Cette mesure permettrait de prévenir l’exode de nouveaux marabouts vers Bamako.

Une étude nigérienne plaidait déjà pour réglementer plutôt que supprimer. Faire appliquer le Code du travail aux aides-ménagères : contrat, salaire minimum, suivi par l'inspection du travail. Les mineures sous l’âge légal doivent être reconduites au village, mais seulement une fois ces conditions créées sur place.

Il faut également préparer le retour avant toute opération des autorités visant à retirer des enfants de la rue. Au Burundi, une étude de 2025 conclut que des retours non préparés n’ont pas empêché les enfants de retourner dans la rue.

Les formalités de l'adoption-protection doivent être assouplies C'est la seule protection que le droit offre à un enfant confié, que les familles modestes fuient, sans céder sur l’intérêt de l’enfant.

Sanctionner et associer

Il faut distinguer pauvreté et exploitation. Le Code pénal de 2024 punit la mendicité et l'incitation d'un mineur à mendier (art. 242-91), plus sévèrement la traite des mineurs, y compris l'exploitation de leur mendicité (art. 324-29, dix ans de réclusion).

Les familles fragiles, comme une mère en détresse qui mendie avec ses enfants, relèvent de l’accompagnement. Ceux qui tirent profit de l’enfant, comme un adulte qui utilise un enfant qui n’est pas le sien, doivent répondre de leurs actes.

Il faut enfin associer les autorités et légitimités traditionnelles, reconnues par la Constitution de ( 2023 ), et les chercheurs, pour un diagnostic préalable et un suivi indépendant.

Au Sénégal, un projet de loi , sur le statut des daara (écoles coraniques), approuvé par les chefs religieux, n'était toujours pas transmis à l'Assemblée en novembre 2024. Un texte approuvé n'est pas un texte appliqué.

Où et quand agir

La question utile n'est pas seulement « comment retirer un enfant de la rue ? », mais « à quel moment aurait-on pu éviter qu'il y arrive ? ». Pour beaucoup d'enfants, la réponse se trouve au village, chez un marabout ou dans une famille tutrice, bien avant le carrefour.

stories.body:
Agriculture in the global south remains under pressure to produce more food while responding to climate change and resource constraints . Policy responses have focused on increasing production. But what about post-harvest losses? Globally, about one-third of food produced for human consumption is estimated to be lost or wasted.

The problem was examined in a recent paper by agriculture, indigenous knowledge and food security researchers.

What are the main drivers of these losses?

Our research was based on examining 324 studies on the scale, causes and drivers of post-harvest losses across food commodities and regions of the global south.

We found that the evidence is fragmented and uneven. In addition, estimating the true scale is difficult because studies measure losses differently. They examine different commodities and stages of the value chain and use different indicators and methods. Research has also concentrated heavily on storage losses in major staples such as maize, rice and pulses. That has left evidence gaps for fruits, vegetables, roots and tubers, animal products and other foods.

But we were able to identify some patterns.

Firstly, post-harvest losses occur throughout the food supply chain, from harvesting and handling to transportation, storage, processing and marketing.

Secondly, there’s substantial variation among food groups. For example, without interventions, estimated losses were about 27.7% of cereals, 35.1% of vegetables, 25.8% of fruits and 42.9% of roots and tubers. With appropriate mitigation measures, such as improved harvesting and handling practices, hermetic storage technologies, cold-chain infrastructure, better packaging, and enhanced processing and transportation systems, these fell to about 8.2%, 7.3%, 6.2% and 11.5%, respectively.

These figures illustrate the scale of variation and the potential for reduction.

Thirdly, post-harvest losses are rarely caused by a single factor. Our study identified interconnected infrastructure, technological, environmental, financial and market constraints.

Poor roads , inadequate warehouses, limited cold storage and inefficient transport expose food to physical damage and spoilage . Inadequate drying, packaging and handling add to these losses. Climate variability increases the risk: high temperatures, excessive moisture, floods and droughts can accelerate deterioration.

What are the four biggest challenges – and opportunities?

First is measuring losses accurately. Before governments can decide where to invest, they need reliable information about where losses occur and how large they are. Standardised, region- and commodity-specific methods for measuring post-harvest losses would make evidence more comparable and help governments target resources more effectively.

Researchers, national statistical agencies, governments, international organisations and commodity-sector stakeholders should work together to develop these methods. National statistical offices, agricultural research institutions, universities, extension services and value-chain organisations can then gather the evidence through:

farm and household surveys

field-based measurement

storage and market assessments

monitoring across different stages of the supply chain.

Read more: Food waste in South Africa is dumped in landfills - study weighs up healthier and more sustainable options

Second is infrastructure that keeps food moving and preserves its quality. Storage facilities, rural roads, processing facilities and cold chains are not secondary agricultural infrastructure. They are part of the food-production system. The evidence shows that improved storage, drying, packaging and cold-chain systems substantially reduce losses, improve farmers’ incomes and increase access to higher-value markets.

Read more: South Africa’s small-scale farmers still can’t find a place in the food value chain

Third is making appropriate technologies affordable and combining them with Indigenous knowledge. Not every solution needs to be high-tech . Hermetic storage (airtight sealing), solar drying, improved packaging and low-cost cooling can complement practices such as drying, smoking, salting and fermentation .

These approaches would be more accessible to smallholders when adapted to local conditions. They can be encouraged through practical demonstrations and locally adapted training. Training avenues include farmer extension services, demonstration farms, farmer organisations and cooperatives, local processors, NGOs, private-sector suppliers and digital platforms.

Fourth is finance, extension and inclusive innovation. Many smallholder farmers lack the finance and technical support needed to invest in improved storage and processing technologies. Price fluctuations and harvest gluts leave farmers with more produce than markets can absorb, increasing the losses of perishable foods before they are sold. Credit constraints can prevent farmers from adopting post-harvest technologies.

Governments and financial institutions can lower barriers through targeted subsidies, affordable loans, grants and risk-sharing machanisms. Extension services should also help farmers choose, use and maintain appropriate technologies.

Women play important roles in post-harvest handling. They need to be explicitly included in technology design, training and financing. This can be done through:

agricultural and financial policies that require women’s representation in technology design and extension programmes

improving their access to credit, subsidies and training

mandated monitoring of how men and women adopt and benefit from technology.

How could priorities be funded?

The evidence suggests that funding shouldn’t only focus on buying technologies. Public investment could support rural infrastructure, research, extension and enabling policies. Development finance could provide grants, concessional loans and guarantees for post-harvest investments. Private-sector partnerships can help with storage, processing , logistics and cold-chain services where viable markets exist.

Read more: Ghana’s rice farmers need finance for new technologies, but banks don’t trust them

Funding should move beyond isolated technology projects such as one-off storage or processing equipment schemes. It should support integrated programmes combining technology, farmer training, finance, market access and maintenance services. Investments should support entire value chains, linking farmers to storage, processing, transport and reliable markets. This would make post-harvest loss reduction part of broader food security, climate resilience and rural development strategies.

Read more: China is funding African farmers but not food processing and storage: why it’s a problem

The central message from our research is simple: feeding a growing population is not only about producing more food. It’s also about losing less of what farmers already produce.

stories.title: Portugal Tests Whether Law Can Constrain Empire
stories.summary: Portuguese prosecutors are investigating whether the U.S. use of the Lajes Air Base for the Iran War was legal. The post Portugal Tests Whether Law Can Constrain Empire appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Luís Montenegro (Shutterstock)

This month, Portuguese prosecutors opened an investigation into whether the center-right government of Prime Minister Luís Montenegro legally authorized the United States to use the Lajes Air Base in the Azores during the war on Iran. The probe was triggered by a complaint from the Left Bloc that opposed the war.

This is the kind of story that has implications beyond Lisbon. At issue is a question: when partners in the Western alliance facilitate American military operations, who decides whether that participation is lawful—and can anyone hold them to account?

A 1951 bilateral defense treaty allows Washington to use Lajes without prior authorization during peacetime. The base is a pillar of the U.S. force-projection architecture, a strategic transit hub hosting the 65th Air Base Wing and supporting U.S., NATO, and allied operations. But once hostilities begin, Portugal must explicitly approve its use.

Unlike neighboring Spain—where Pedro Sánchez’s center-left government refused the use of U.S. bases to attack Iran and condemned the war as contrary to international law—Lisbon authorized several U.S. transit flights through the base. That decision drew sharp criticism from left-wing parties and ignited a domestic debate over Portugal’s complicity in a conflict it insists it is not part of.

Reacting to the launched inquiry, Prime Minister Montenegro defended Lisbon’s decision, arguing that the use of the base was “fully legal” and urged the judiciary “not to make political judgements.” Earlier, Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said that he considered “everything done to re-open the Hormuz Strait and secure the maritime freedom as a positive,” while emphasizing that Portugal was not involved. And recently, on a visit to Lisbon, standing alongside his Portuguese counterpart, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted that Washington had “adhered to the protocols” regulating the use of the base.

Unlike in some other countries, where prosecutors enjoy broad discretion to decline cases, in Portugal they are bound by the principle of legality: they must investigate when there are sufficient grounds. Contrary to Montenegro’s insinuations , the investigation is not a political stunt. It is the law working as designed.

That is precisely why the probe is worth watching—and why it may ultimately disappoint.

“It is a good thing that it’s being scrutinised, but plenty of things get scrutinized to no avail,” notes, in an interview from Lisbon, Ghoncheh Tazmini, author of Power Couple: Russian-Iranian Alignment in the Middle East , a Fellow of the UK-based Royal Historical Society, and currently working on a book on the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s a deeper political reality that determines these matters, regardless of the legal arguments.”

That deeper reality is worth naming. As Tazmini puts it: “Portugal’s response illustrates the gap between formal sovereignty and genuine strategic autonomy. Despite its legal authority to impose conditions (on the use of Lajes), Lisbon has shown little willingness to depart from Washington’s strategic priorities, revealing how deeply entrenched alliance dependencies continue to shape Portuguese foreign policy.”

Ana Gomes , a retired Portuguese diplomat and a former presidential candidate , is even more direct. She rejects the government’s legal justification outright. “Abundant evidence demonstrates that President Trump’s actions against Iran were neither defensive nor proportionate. They were illegal acts of aggression, clearly violating the UN Charter and international law”, she said to FPIF. She calls the Portuguese government’s position “mere disingenuous hypocrisy to dismiss questions.”

Gomes points to a telling admission. “Rubio declared last May to Fox News that the Portuguese authorization was obtained by the United States ‘even before Portugal was informed about what would be the U.S. request.'” For Gomes, this “clearly shows that Portugal preferred not to know.”

She is equally skeptical that the investigation will produce accountability, invoking a precedent that haunts Portuguese debates over complicity in American operations. Portugal’s governments under Prime Ministers Durão Barroso (center-right) and José Sócrates (center-left) authorized the CIA’s rendition program under President George W. Bush “war on terror.” The program abducted “illegal combatants” and transported them to U.S.-controlled sites for interrogations that included torture. Portugal’s airspace and airports were heavily utilized to facilitate the illegal transfer and kidnapping of terrorism suspects.

As a former member of the European Parliament, Ana Gomes played a key role in exposing that complicity. That experience doesn’t make her feel optimistic about the Iran war probe: “At some point the attorney general will order closure, to serve the government, regardless of the collected evidence of human rights and international law violations and the government and state officials responsible for them.”

Gomes also disputes the premise that Portugal’s choices should always be determined by its strategic dependence on Washington. “Portugal has a strategic dependence on the integrity and reinforcement of the European Union, as its member state, not on the United States”, she said to FPIF.

The subservience, she argues, “serves the interests—namely economic interests—of parts of Lisbon’s establishment, both political and military,” now compounded by “fear of facing the erratic retaliations and bullying from the Trump administration, be it tariffs, disputes over NATO financial contributions or claims over some strategic territory of the allies (in a thinly-veiled reference to the Azores archipelago in the Atlantic).” Unlike Sánchez, she adds,

Portugal’s leadership believes that by appeasing Trump it might escape his ire.

Yet the Lajes probe still matters, for three reasons.

First, it exposes the fiction that junior partners are mere bystanders. Portugal did not object to the flights. It made a choice. The investigation forces Lisbon to defend that choice in legal terms, not just diplomatic ones—and that is a form of accountability, however partial.

Second, it highlights the asymmetry embedded in the Atlantic alliance. The United States can use bases, transit airspace, and stage operations with assurances that are often unverifiable. Portugal, meanwhile, absorbs the political and legal risk.

Third, it connects to a deeper question about European strategic autonomy. In her tenure in the European Parliament, Gomes recalls, she was pushing to develop the EU’s own security and defense capabilities. Instead, she argues, “the military and political establishments in several member states resisted it, pretending that NATO alone could take care of our defense.”

That, in effect, has sealed Europe’s self-vassalization. If a superpower can use a junior partner’s territory to wage an illegal war without any effective limits and verification, sovereignty becomes hollow. The Lajes controversy is but one symptom of this larger disease—just like the rendition flights were a decade ago.

And yet, the probe is a revealing test. Its fate will determine whether a 1951 treaty and a prosecutor’s obligation to investigate can meaningfully constrain a superpower—or whether, as history suggests, the deeper political reality will prevail again.

stories.title: Arctic Wildlife Research Suffers as Geopolitical Competition Grows
stories.summary: As national security and the hunt for rare minerals come to dominate Arctic agendas, governments are slashing support for wildlife research. Scientists say the loss of monitoring is unprecedented and comes as climate change dramatically reshapes life in the Far North. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A polar bear on sea ice in the Arctic Ocean. Sebnem Coskun / Anadolu via Getty Images

As national security and the hunt for rare minerals come to dominate Arctic agendas, governments are slashing support for wildlife research. Scientists say the loss of monitoring is unprecedented and comes as climate change dramatically reshapes life in the Far North.

By Ed Struzik • October 15, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Decades ago, one of the world’s largest subpopulations of nesting eider ducks spent its summers on tiny Mitivik Island, near the mouth of Hudson Bay. But as concern grew, in the 1990s, over their steep decline globally, the Canadian government set up a rudimentary research station near the island in the hopes of forestalling a collapse.

The modest investment paid enormous dividends over the next 30 years as Inuit partners from nearby Southampton Island, who hunt common and king eiders for food and feathers, worked with scientists from all over the world to solve the mystery of where the birds spent their winters and the causes of, and remedy for, their initial decline. In the field for months at a time, researchers also gained critical insights into how climate change, disease, diminishing sea ice, and polar bears were affecting bird populations.

As remarkably successful as the pioneering research station was, though, Canada’s Environment and Climate Change department quietly shut it down in 2024. By then, the number of nesting eiders had crashed again, from a high of 8,000 pairs to just a few hundred.

Today, federal research continues in only three of the 14 migratory bird sanctuaries in the Arctic. Hundreds of other wildlife research endeavors in the circumpolar world, including in Greenland and the U.S., have also been shuttered in recent years.

Support for Arctic research has always ebbed and flowed, says a scientist. “But what we are seeing now is unprecedented.”

Like many other agencies and programs operated by Environment and Climate Change Canada, the Canadian Wildlife Service has suffered from the high cost of conducting research in the Arctic, the increasing likelihood of polar bear encounters as sea ice recedes, and a series of crushing funding cuts. In the most recent blow, the Canadian government in 2025 committed to reducing the Environment and Climate Change workforce by 10 percent .

In the past, funding to monitor wildlife in the Arctic often had to be justified by its relevance to oil and gas development and how roads, pipelines, and oil wells would affect animals such as migrating caribou, according to Larry Hinzman, an expert in Arctic change at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. But as the search for Arctic oil and gas began to ramp down in the late 2000s, due to low natural gas prices and breakthroughs in fracking for oil and gas that spurred new production in the south, climate change became a priority.

The current circumpolar decline in funding, Hinzman said, is not just about rising costs. It stems from governments shifting priorities once again, this time from climate change to national security issues and the search for rare minerals. According to the Harvard Kennedy School’s Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, geopolitical tensions are also undermining the work of the Arctic Council, an international forum comprising the eight Arctic countries that plays a key role in monitoring environmental changes in the region.

Wildlife technician Uli Steiner tags a king eider netted on Mitivik Island before research efforts were halted in 2024. Grant Gilchrist

While support for research in the Arctic wanes, Canada is investing $405 million to advance the construction of a new highway to the Arctic coast to facilitate resource development and connect remote communities, part of a $40 billion plan to assert sovereignty over its Arctic territory.

Research in Alaska has been particularly hard hit by the suspension of hundreds of climate-based collaborations with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, and by the closure last year of the Arctic Research Consortium of the United States after the National Science Foundation eliminated its operating grants. Between 2021 and 2024, the number of U.S. research publications on climate change in Greenland fell by 32 percent . And in July the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the territory’s leading environmental research center, temporarily halted any new collaboration with U.S. partners when President Donald Trump threatened to take over the island.

“There have always been ebbs and flows in the support for environmental monitoring in the Arctic,” said Hinzman. “But what we are seeing now is unprecedented. It’s heartbreaking because we need to know more than ever how to respond to a warming Arctic that is affecting almost every facet of life.”

The decline in Arctic research comes at a time when at least 96 Arctic and sub-Arctic mammal and bird species may be responding to warmer winters, earlier spring snowmelt, and profound landscape changes by migrating earlier in the year and traveling farther afield, sometimes in new directions.

Studies from a now shuttered Hudson Bay research station led to tighter regulations on hunting that fueled an eider resurgence.

But dozens of studies have shown that these journeys don’t always lead to more food. And they often expose birds to additional parasites and pathogens and put them at greater risk of predation. The new migrations also happen at a time when critical stopover sites — like the Salton Sea, in California — are being badly degraded by drought and development.

Polar bears and eiders are among the many animals that appear to be struggling with rapidly warming northern marine environments, from the Baltic to the Canadian Arctic Ocean to the eastern seaboard , stretching from Newfoundland to Maine. But without researchers in the field, it’s difficult to predict how or whether these species may adapt.

The situation was far different when eiders began their mysterious worldwide decline in the 1990s. Then, researchers working in Mitivik, in the East Bay Migratory Bird Sanctuary, which would later be named the Qaqsauqtuuq Migratory Bird Sanctuary, implanted satellite transmitters into the abdomens of eiders and learned where they were overwintering. The findings led to tighter regulations on eider hunting in Canada and Greenland that dramatically boosted eider numbers.

That is, until they crashed again due to disease and polar bear predation. In 2005, Grant Gilchrist, the founder of the research station, and his colleagues identified an outbreak of avian cholera — which is rare in the Arctic and likely linked to global warming — that would kill as many as 3,000 nesting females in 2006 and about half the population over the eight seasons it spread through the nesting colony.

U.S. soldiers conduct cold-weather training near Fairbanks, Alaska, in February, after President Trump threatened to invade Greenland. Victor J. Blue / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Gilchrist was also on hand to witness how receding sea ice, brought on by climate change, forced polar bears onto land just when the eiders were sitting on their eggs. “The bears were like grazing cows leisurely moving through a pasture, stopping to feed [on eggs] whenever they were hungry,” he said. And herring gulls, which can’t force an eider off its nest, learned to eat the eggs that the bears had missed while the eiders were away.

Canadian Wildlife Service scientist Jennifer Provencher and her colleagues discovered that even though the eiders nesting in Mitivik hosted larger-than-expected communities of gastrointestinal worms and flukes, which benefit from warming temperatures, the parasites reduced the ducks’ exposure to contaminants such as mercury and lead. The parasites appear to absorb and clear contaminants from eider tissues. This is significant because mercury and lead, which are leaching from melting permafrost in many parts of the Arctic, can result in reproductive failure in ducks, and they can be harmful to humans who rely on ducks for food. The Inuit have higher levels of mercury than the general Canadian population.

Other researchers found that eiders, like some other animals exposed to deadly disease, eventually developed an immunity to avian cholera.

“Had we not been there, we would never have been able to document any of this,” said Gilchrist, who says he has little doubt that most of what Mitivik researchers discovered is happening in other parts of the Arctic.

Determining how polar bears are faring in Canada is becoming difficult, if not impossible, because of a lack of funding, a scientist says.

In the past, Indigenous hunters have reported dramatic changes in the Canadian Arctic, such as sharp declines in ivory gull numbers; orcas moving into the region and killing narwhal and bowhead whales; and grizzly bears migrating north, mating with polar bears, and producing hybrids. But it is almost impossible to say what is going on in the vast areas that are too far afield for Inuit hunters without putting scientists in the field. In Arctic Canada, there are approximately 150,000 people living in an area that is about half the size of the Lower 48 states. Only a fraction of these people lives above the Arctic Circle.

Environment and Climate Change Canada did not respond to questions about funding cuts and the cessation of research in Mitivik. In a statement, the department said it is “committed to the long-term conservation of biological biodiversity and abundance,” noting that experts are working on new research programs with territorial governments and Indigenous organizations, and with new technologies to help track and understand birds and other animals, including polar bears.

Still, Andrew Derocher, a University of Alberta scientist who has conducted research over the past 40 years on polar bears in Norway, Canada, and Alaska, notes that support for polar bear research in Canada is at an all-time low. Determining how polar bears are faring in Canada — which is home to 13 of the world’s 19 polar bear populations — is becoming increasingly difficult, he says, if not impossible, because of a lack of government funding.

Eiders found dead after an avian cholera outbreak on Mitivik Island in 2006. Grant Gilchrist

“We’ve pretty much stopped any research beyond the long-term monitoring in Western Hudson Bay and a project in James Bay” funded by a private foundation, he says. “There is almost no other research on polar bears in Canada now.”

Ornithologist Mark Mallory spent 12 years conducting research at migratory bird nesting sites across the Canadian Arctic while working for the Canadian Wildlife Service, but he left that job for a research chair at Acadia University in part because of the high cost of conducting research in the polar regions and the endless struggle to secure consistent funding. Mallory is still very much interested in what is happening in the Arctic, but his years in the field and as co-editor-in-chief of the journal Arctic Science have given him a broader perspective on the challenges scientists face when trying to figure out how a warming climate is affecting wildlife.

“No credible scientist would deny that not enough is being invested in long-term monitoring,” he says. “But the bigger problem is not enough is being done to act on what we know is happening… Do we really think 10 or 20 more years of data showing ranges shrinking north, or clutch sizes reducing, or skinnier species is going to change anything in the minds of politicians or the public?”

Gilchrist appreciates Mallory’s frustrations with governments that refuse to act on climate change, but he — like many Arctic researchers — still believes that long-term monitoring with Inuit partners is essential. “Somebody should still be out in nature monitoring wildlife and the natural environment, and quantifying changes that are occurring or not occurring,” he said.

He doesn’t know whether the eiders of Mitivik Island will eventually return or whether they have found safer areas to nest. Because of the high costs of operating at Qaqsauqtuuq and the increased odds of running into polar bears, Gilchrist is now focusing his research at a site on Baffin Island, where it is cheaper to work and where there are fewer bears.

stories.title: Thailand Hosts a Controversial Guest
stories.summary: The World Bank and IMF are meeting this week in Thailand. The Thai people are not enthusiastic. The post Thailand Hosts a Controversial Guest appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Pak Mun Dam (Shutterstock)

Perhaps the two international agencies that would score lowest in popularity among Thais would be the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. This is why many Thais have greeted with consternation the news that these sister agencies will be holding their 2026 fall meeting in Bangkok from October 12 to 18.

Mention the World Bank, and the first thing that comes to mind in this country is the Pak Mun Dam. In December 1991, the Bank provided a $24 million loan to help fund the $250 million hydroelectric dam constructed by the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT). To build the massive structure, about 1700 households were dislocated. After it went into operation, the dam ended up blocking fish migration from the Mekong River, causing a catastrophic 60-80 percent loss of fish species and destroying the livelihoods of over 20,000 local fisherfolk. Over the last three decades, the balance of costs and benefits have been clearly weighted towards costs, so that the affected communities continue to advocate decommissioning it.

The Pak Mun Dam is just one example of the mega-dam projects that have displaced millions and earned the Bank a bad name in international civil society. According to the International Rivers Network, until around 1993, the Bank had made 527 dam-related loans for the construction, expansion, or rehabilitation of dams in 93 countries. The Bank has also come under fire for the billions it has spent supporting fossil-fuel projects throughout the Global South. Over the last few years, the Bank has extended at least $21 billion for coal, oil, and gas energy projects despite the worsening impact of climate change.

The Pak Mun debacle is not the only problem associated with the Bank in Thailand. In 1997, during the Asian Financial Crisis that was caused partly by their pressure to liberalize the country’s capital account, the Bank and the IMF contributed $5.5 billion toward a $17.2 billion “rescue fund,” which was used not to rescue Thais suffering from the crisis but to reimburse foreign investors and speculators that had lost their money. To pay off the loan consortium, the government raised the value added tax (VAT) from seven to 10 percent, causing severe economic suffering, provoking a deep recession, and plunging one million Thais below the poverty line in a few short weeks.

“Attacking” Poverty While Living in the Lap of Luxury

In recent years, the Bank has defined its mission as ending poverty in the developing world. To fulfill this goal, its lending has risen from nearly $55 billion in 2015 to $123 billion in 2026. But if ending global poverty is universally regarded as a worthy cause, why is the World Bank so controversial?

To manage its operations, the Bank’s full-time staff increased from nearly 12,000 in 2015 to over 20,758 full-time staff globally in 2026. These figures are just the tip of the iceberg. If one includes all employees—permanent, non-permanent, contractual, part-time—throughout the world, the Bank employs close to 41,000 people. The vast majority, 26,000, or 63 percent, work out of the World Bank headquarters in Washington, DC, enjoying tax-free salaries, while only 3,200 are located in Africa, the location of the vast number of people classified as living in extreme poverty.

The Bank’s economists and top administrators are among the highest paid financial functionaries in the world, which explains why the Bank is a major cause of the brain drain from developing countries: a great number of highly trained economists from developing countries prefer to work at the Bank instead of their home countries, with some going straight from Ivy League or British graduate schools to Washington, DC.

Despite the massive increase in personnel, the Bank admits that global poverty reduction “has slowed to a near standstill, with 2020-2030 set to be a lost decade.” Some 3.5 billion people, or 44 percent of the globe, remain poor, after decades of massive World Bank lending. And a major part of the reason, critics say, is that World Bank programs have created poverty instead of alleviating it.

The Bank and Structural Adjustment Programs

Central to the creation of global poverty and inequality has been the World Bank and IMF’s “structural adjustment,” the austerity programs guided by the radical principles of the “Washington Consensus.” Structural adjustment is a program that promotes trade liberalization, deregulation, and privatization, along with severe cuts in government spending. Its goal is supposedly to promote growth and reduce poverty.

Over 100 developing and post-socialist countries have been brought under World Bank and IMF structural adjustment regimes. Yet over the last 47 years, there have been few or no successes at all, so that many countries remain under adjustment indefinitely, becoming, in effect, permanent wards of the two institutions. Very few developing countries graduate from structural adjustment.

At its height in the 1980s and 1990s, structural adjustment programs accounted for 20-30 percent of total World Bank lending. But so meager were the positive results of the program that it was renamed the “Poverty Reduction Strategy Program.” However, investigations, such as those that our organization Focus on the Global South conducted on adjustment programs in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, saw the so-called reform of structural adjustment as no more than sugar-coating: “The PRSP is upheld by the World Bank and the IMF as a comprehensive approach. That is certainly is, but not for poverty reduction. The PRSP is a comprehensive program for structural adjustment, in the name of the poor.”

Expert Panel: World Bank Policies Based on Questionable Findings

The reason that World Bank projects and programs don’t work or create exactly the opposite of their intended goals is because they are based on questionable propositions built on little or no empirical evidence. An assessment made a few years ago by an all-star team of renowned economists led by Princeton’s Angus Deaton, a recipient of the Nobel Prize for Economics, was damning:

[The] panel had substantial criticisms of the way that the research was used to proselytize on behalf of Bank policy, often without taking a balanced view, and without expressing appropriate skepticism. Internal research that is favorable to Bank positions was given great prominence, and unfavorable research ignored. In these cases, we believe that there was a serious failure of checks and balances that should have separated advocacy and research. The panel endorses the right of the Bank to strongly defend and advocate its own policies. But when the Bank leadership selectively appeals to relatively new and untested research as hard evidence that these preferred policies work, it lends unwarranted confidence to the Bank’s prescriptions. Placing fragile selected new research results on a pedestal invites later recrimination that undermines the credibility and usefulness of all Bank research.

Austerity and Hierarchy

Some economists are more critical, like the noted Italian economist Clara Mattei, who claims that the reason for the failure of austerity or adjustment programs is that they are meant to fail. She contends that, though cloaked in the language of scientific economics, the aim of the paradigm is not to restore economic growth or achieve popular well-being but to reinforce a class hierarchy or “capital order” that is under siege from below.

“Much economic research has established that austerity has almost never worked as promised, neither stimulating growth nor reducing debt,” she writes. “So why does it continue to be the preferred course of action for governments? We cannot simply attribute its structural presence to the stupidity or corruption of those in government. The true measure of austerity’s effectiveness is its ability to impose of reinforce a class structure, the very order that underpins economic growth. In this sense , austerity has never been an irrational calculation.”

The Bank’s refusal to acknowledge real-world refutations of its pro-globalization advocacy and its unbalanced, one-sided research led to justifiable rejection of its advice by the people who were suffering from the policies it was implementing, confessed Paul Collier, head of the Bank’s Research Development Department of the Bank from 1998 to 2003:

The profession has been unprofessional, fearful that any criticism would strengthen populism, so that little work has been done on the downsides of these different processes [of globalization]. Yet the downsides were apparent to ordinary citizens, and the effect of economists appearing to dismiss them has resulted in widespread refusal of people to listen to “experts.” For my profession to re-establish credibility we must provide a more balanced analysis, in which the downsides are acknowledged and properly evaluated with a view to designing policy responses that address them. The profession may be better served by mea culpa than by further indignant defenses of globalization.

From EOI to AI

Recently, the Bank has been trashed for advocating export-oriented industrialization (EOI), or focusing on turning out products not for the domestic market but for developed country markets. Since the early 1970s the Bank kept telling countries in the Global South that export-oriented industrialization was the way to go. Now, with the Trump administration imposing high tariffs on some 100 countries, this advice has proved disastrous. Developing economies have been totally unprepared for this, so that owing to a lack of an alternative model to the export-oriented growth model in an era of protectionism in northern markets, they are scrambling for new paradigms.

Now the World Bank is promoting another silver bullet for Thailand: artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven-growth. The Bank is pushing this despite a grim warning from its sister agency, the IMF, that in emerging markets and low-income countries, AI is expected to negatively affect 40 percent and 26 percent of jobs, respectively. “Many of these countries,” says the Fund, “don’t have the infrastructure or skilled workforces to harness the benefits of AI, raising the risk that over time the technology could worsen inequality among nations.”

But mass unemployment and ecological disruptions by data centers do not pose the only, or even the most serious, threat to countries like Thailand. It is disconcerting that the Bank is speaking in glowing terms about AI when leading AI firms like ChatGPT and Anthropic are now saying that AI’s development and adoption should be reined in owing to the “existential threat” (that is, extinction) that advanced AI programs pose to humanity.

The Law of Bureaucratic Inertia

Despite the high rate of failure of its lending programs acknowledged in internal World Bank assessments, the World Bank administrative budget that supports the high salaries of its economists and other high-level staff just keeps growing. The World Bank (IBRD/IDA) administrative budget was approved at $3.6 billion for FY26, a sizable rise from the $2.8 billion authorized for FY 2021, or nearly $800 million, with no convincing reason at all.

To many it seems strange that an organization keeps growing despite obviously failing in its mission. Sociologists are not surprised, seeing this as the operation of the “law of bureaucratic inertia,” or the tendency of organizations to expand even when they have become irrelevant or counterproductive. In other words, the fundamental objective of the Bank is to grow and perpetuate itself, not eliminate global poverty. The means have become the end.

A number of our friends who have worked at the World Bank in Washington have told us that, as one of them put it, “if you join the Bank, you will never be fired, you’ll continually be promoted, and your salary will continue to rise even if you put in minimal work.” This is probably an exaggeration, but it asserts something that is essentially true. Workers said of the old so-called socialist regimes of Eastern Europe: “They pretend to pay us, and we pretend to work.” The same apparently can be said of the highly-paid massive bureaucracy at the World Bank.

In this regard, defunding the World Bank is one area where the agendas of the right and the left coincide, though for different reasons—the right because it thinks the Bank is wasting money, the left because it is convinced that the Bank is doing harm to the people and the planet.

stories.title: Scientists Are Teaching Birds to Sing Lost Songs
stories.summary: When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
This article was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A rufous-collared sparrow. Charles J. Sharp via Wikipedia

When bird populations decline, fledglings may struggle to learn the songs they need to attract mates. But new research suggests it is possible to teach birds lost songs.

Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area.

That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.

There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect,” they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory, and ultimately survive.

If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers. Birds can begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species , jeopardizing their chances of breeding.

Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well — which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently, and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy, you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo.

“When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B. Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who coauthored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds .

But animals’ learned behavior or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin.

The rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist.

About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows, and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds, has identified common “motifs” or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes, and harmonic notes.

The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range.

The song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out.

It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined.

Birds’ songs can change naturally over time — for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes.

Songbirds learn from other members of their species — such as a father or neighbors — which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge.

“There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behavior at the University of Plymouth, who studied a group of cirl buntings that were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project.

Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal.

A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says.

Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated.

A separate study in Australia tracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation.

“Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins.

Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that A.I. could help provide live tutoring in the future.

Dialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarizing birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this.

A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.”

In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists.

— Rebecca Ratcliffe , The Guardian
