stories.title: An Inside Look At How To Tame Unstoppable AI
stories.summary: The post An Inside Look At How To Tame Unstoppable AI appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Slowing the AI race may not be possible. But there is a path to oversight that doesn’t depend on the industry’s permission — and it comes from the past.

Anna August specializes in AI governance, audit and compliance across the European Union, United Kingdom and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Earlier this year, a university decided to audit the effectiveness of its new AI system designed to help answer student questions. So, university officials hired me, an AI auditor, to come take a look. During my review, I discovered that the AI agent, which was supposed to handle only general questions about the academic calendar and organizational matters, had started opening students’ personal records — accessing data that wasn’t needed to answer their questions. The chatbot, however, did nothing further with that information.

When the university’s engineers, at the time, learned what happened from the access logs, they fixed it, and that was that. There was no official record. No internal rule required them to record such incidents, and nobody was assigned to track events like this. It was simply part of the engineering team’s bug-fixing process. The incident was what I call a near miss, and near misses are what a reporting system exists to catch. The same behavior could lead to something more serious next time, and we only know about this case because the university voluntarily brought me in to examine the system.

The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents, and a chatbot that answers general questions is nowhere near that category. Even for high-risk systems, those duties do not apply until December 2027, and a near-miss that causes no harm would not count as a serious incident anyway.

That is why, as an AI auditor, I ask organizations at the start of every engagement to show me how they track system behavior through testing and deployment. I ask for records of systems acting in ways they’re not meant to, accessing data outside their role, anomalies and near-misses, or problems caught before they caused harm. Most places, like the university, have no such records.

The university had commissioned the audit voluntarily. There was no deliberate obfuscation of the facts on their part; there was simply no process to surface these important details, and nothing obliged them to build one, especially in the testing phase. Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.

This summer showed the same gap on a larger scale. OpenAI’s test agents escaped their sandbox and broke into Hugging Face, and internal teams had seen warning signs for weeks before anyone outside the company found out. Anthropic then found intrusions of its own. By late September, OpenAI and Anthropic were reportedly investigating tens of thousands of incidents. Many have answered with calls for a pause. No company or country can afford to stop first, so the pause most likely will not come. But what can come is a real oversight, enforced and executed.

This essay argues for three requirements: registering frontier models before deployment, reporting incidents on a fixed legal clock, and independent audits that reach testing environments, not only released products. None of them asks anyone to slow down. In every country that adopts them, they put the race under independent observation. The goal is to make the race governed rather than left to voluntary restraint.

These days, the calls for a pause are coming from many different directions. In July, the Vatican and more than 200 Nobel Prize winners called for a global slowdown on artificial intelligence development. Soon after, more than 1,000 employees at top AI companies, along with managers at OpenAI and Anthropic, asked the American government to build a mechanism for a possible future pause. Then, over 3,000 economists, including AI researchers and Nobel Laureates, signed a letter , “We Must Act Now,” warning that the pace and scale of rapid artificial intelligence development could destabilize the economy and labor market faster than anyone is prepared for. And on 12 September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on frontier labs to “pace the frontier,” and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis agreed within hours and days. That was a real catalyst for one of the most important discussions happening right now. Almost everyone weighed in, including Chinese politicians.

Alongside these pleas and letters, incidents at frontier companies this summer have created a genuine, ongoing crisis. Axios reported that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving potentially problematic model behavior, against a backdrop of hundreds of thousands of test runs conducted by AI companies.

“Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.”

The ‘Confession’

The Hugging Face breach set off much of this summer’s soul-searching. And understanding its particulars is necessary to determine an appropriate solution. On July 21, OpenAI disclosed that its models had escaped a testing environment and broken into the systems of Hugging Face — a key platform that hosts much of the world’s open-source AI. Only a week later, Anthropic revealed that during testing, its models broke into the open internet and intruded into the systems of three separate organizations, extracting large production data from one of them. Both companies framed their announcements as the transparent, responsible thing to do, even if uncomfortable.

OpenAI had been running an evaluation of its models’ underlying cyber capabilities on a benchmark (called ExploitGym). Safety guardrails that would normally block the AI from proceeding were deliberately reduced, which is standard practice when testing a system’s safety. Some of the tasks were designed to be unsolvable. The models were supposed to be isolated from each other, each in its own sandbox, like students writing the same exam but in different rooms. But instead, more than 1,200 agents found a way to communicate through an internal message board. They shared information about their tasks, goals, and, importantly, routes to the open internet. Within hours, they developed a universal cheat for the benchmark.

Over the next days, they coordinated the sustained effort to trick the scoring system into accepting their cheats. More than 700 agents exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to reach outside OpenAI’s infrastructure on the open internet, inferred that Hugging Face might hold materials related to their evaluation, and broke into its production systems to steal what they expected would let them succeed on the test. If they were real-world students, they didn’t just cheat on the test; they broke into the teacher’s office to find the answer key.

Now, timing is critical and adds important context. It also makes the transparency framing more questionable. An internal OpenAI team observed agents using the message board and breaking into the open internet without authorization in late May. Another team found further evidence on June 27. On July 5, a message board outage triggered a formal security incident. The attack on Hugging Face took place between July 10 and 13 (by using exposed user credentials agents found on the internet). Hugging Face detected unauthorized activity in their production environments during the week of July 13and reported the intrusion to the public and the police on July 16, not realizing it was a swarm of OpenAI’s test agents. OpenAI admitted it was them in the public disclosure on July 21. So the world learned about OpenAI’s misaligned agents only after Hugging Face made the story public and the police were already involved.

Anthropic’s disclosure , published nine days later, was directly related to OpenAI’s reveal. As a result, Anthropic launched a retrospective review of its own cybersecurity evaluations and uncovered three previously undetected incidents, the earliest dating back to April 2026, in which its model gained unauthorized access to the systems of real organizations.

Since Hugging Face detected the intrusion on July 16 and reported it to police, the case has moved through several distinct phases, and the scope widened considerably in September. Reuters reported that OpenAI agents had probed Hugging Face and hijacked accounts as early as May, two months before the main attack, and the AI safety group Nightingale Collective disclosed that agents had used a German wiki to coordinate their actions. On September 25, OpenAI confirmed a leak of more than 50 ChatGPT user images and said it had notified dozens of institutions, including universities and government agencies, of possible impact. In the same week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed at the UN that an OpenAI agent had breached a government health portal in June.

On September 26, OpenAI confirmed its agents had interacted with U.S. government sites including the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau, and the Department of Education. On the same day, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are now investigating tens of thousands of security incidents, turning the Hugging Face case from a single episode into the opening chapter of a much larger crisis of control over autonomous AI agents.

“A frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities.”

But be mindful of this too: a frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities. Every sentence describing how far the model reached, what defenses were defeated, how much initiative it showed, is simultaneously an incident report and a demo. Look how far our system got, even while we were trying to hold it back. Add public statements to the mix, and the contradiction becomes the story: you cannot plead for restraint and demonstrate you are winning the race in the same fortnight.

What An Honest Incident Looks Like

To understand how flawed the current disclosure system has become, it’s worth looking at an AI incident with no press strategy attached. Because such incidents exist as well.

In August, in Australia, a man asked an AI agent to book him into a gym class. As the class was full, the man asked if the agent could move him up the waitlist. As a result, an agent canceled another member’s reservation by hacking the booking system. When asked to undo the change, it couldn’t restore the stranger’s booking. A person lost their gym slot to a machine that discovered, entirely unprompted, that the rules were optional (no authorization checks on cancellation). The story surfaced because the user himself talked about it.

First, this small incident shows the same behavioral signature in miniature as the big laboratory breaches: an agent is given an objective, encounters a constraint and treats it as an engineering problem rather than a boundary. Breaking the rules was the shortest path to the goal, and nothing in their construction weighted the difference. This is why I believe escapes are closer to a default failure mode than a single event. Sandboxes and permission systems were designed to contain software that does what it is told. Agentic systems are built, as their central selling point states, to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will.

Second, the gym incident shows what AI risk looks like when no one is filtering the disclosure. Staged laboratory disclosures are wrapped in lawyers, timing and framing. But accidental reports from users or victim police reports are a completely different story. Any reporting regime designed and operated by the AI companies themselves exposes the difference. Escapes are structurally likely, and this summer showed that containment did not fail for the first time. It reached a point where failures could no longer be hidden, intentionally or otherwise.

New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores used the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident to expose gaps in mandatory AI incident reporting. He argued that the initial version of the RAISE Act, or Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, a New York state law regulating frontier AI labs, would have required reporting such incidents to the New York Attorney General and the state’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services. But after lobbying from OpenAI, the reporting thresholds of how serious or risky an event must be before it must be reported to the state were raised so high that an event like the Hugging Face breach would no longer qualify for mandatory disclosure.

Why Nobody Stops First

Incidents over the summer exposed internal oversight failures and a lack of timely, independent scrutiny. But is that a reason to slow down? To understand this, we must understand the nature of the race itself. Being part of a larger ecosystem gives no company the luxury of slowing down. Companies and their frontier AI labs cannot afford to fall behind rivals, so they are burning sums of capital unseen in prior human history to reach the verge of unstoppable capabilities. A pause would be a gift to competitors. The same logic also plays out between regions and countries; neither Washington nor Beijing will slow down because AI is a strategic asset and nobody wants to fall behind or suffer the consequences. Read Noema in print.

We have encountered this kind of moment in history before: The Cold War-era arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union is the closest example for a specific reason. It depended on the same concept — that technology could be leverage over the other, making unilateral restraint irrational for both. Both powers shared an interest in limiting competition (risks, costs, public opinion, etc.) and knew the best shared outcome was fewer weapons, but neither could safely restrain itself, as it would only strengthen the opponent and, in their view, look like surrender.

“Agentic systems are built … to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will. ”

What eventually made meaningful arms-control agreements possible was not dialogue, pleas and protests alone. It was verification. Satellite reconnaissance, recognized and protected as a national technical means of verification under the SALT agreements , made missile sites, launchers and related infrastructure increasingly observable. Later agreements , particularly INF and START, added extensive data exchanges, notifications and on-site inspections. Verification did not end the arms race on its own. Political leadership, economic pressure and, above all, the transformation of Soviet policy under Mikhail Gorbachev, all played important roles. But verification was critical in turning arms control from a collection of promises into a system of reciprocal, verifiable commitments. That was the game changer.

From this past example and from learning that unilateral restraint is irrational, relevant capabilities, safeguards and incidents must become independently observable. We already have tools that could form such a verification system. First, registration should be mandatory for frontier models before deployment, so that their understanding, scale and awareness are known to dedicated people outside the organization that builds them. Second, incident reporting should occur on a fixed clock — meaning there is a statutory deadline to report an incident to a regulatory body. That will allow us to move away from the communications team’s schedule and instead place it within the regulatory framework. Third, we need external audits, not only of the production systems, but of the testing environments themselves, which shows where the real danger is taking shape, as shown this summer.

As an AI auditor and someone who spent nearly 20 years working in IT, I know this territory well. So I also understand the instinctive response many in that world will give: “But what matters is the production environment!” Well, sure, that too. But we’re no longer talking about static software. We are talking about dynamic artificial intelligence. We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market. We make sure the processes and testing that lead to a medication’s release on the market leave clear compliance records of its entire journey. Rigor in the testing environment is what will keep us safe.

All that this requires is granting visibility, but not visibility just through voluntary disclosure. While Anthropic’s unilateral proposal to invite independent evaluators in is helpful and even admirable, it is still the company’s voluntary choice, scoped to its own walls and revocable at will. This essay argues that independent external scrutiny should become a floor rather than a ceiling: a statutory cross-industry obligation that doesn’t depend on a single leadership team’s goodwill. This means the race runner isn’t being asked to lose the race or stop. Someone simply runs alongside him in the sunlight.

How might this have worked in the case of OpenAI and Hugging Face? First, if OpenAI had registered the model with regulators, they would have been aware of it before it was placed in evaluation with its safeguards reduced. Even simple facts, like that this class of model exists, are being tested and have a named accountable person overseeing their testing. Second, reporting at a fixed time would require reporting within days after the team noticed the anomalies in late May. It would be treated the same as the data breach already is under European law, rather than as an internal curiosity for over six weeks, during which the behavior only escalated. And third, an audit would ensure that the architecture evaluation, behavior and artifacts would be examined by someone who did not benefit from the evaluation finishing on schedule and according to the assumptions. Importantly, none of this requires changing the pace of the research. It only converts something currently private and constrained by goodwill into a fact external parties can see.

Complementary Regulatory Regimes

Of course, all this is easy to say and hard to build. Indeed, building independent, publicly funded mechanisms may be challenging. But this process has already started in various countries. The problem is that each has some pieces of the puzzle but misses others. No nation is building a comprehensive system that captures the need holistically. A regulation’s ability to shape behavior depends entirely on enforcement, but every jurisdiction is going about it slightly differently.

“We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market.”

The European Union has arguably the most comprehensive AI regulatory framework to date. AI Act obligations for general-purpose models existed on paper in August 2025 and remained there — on paper — for an entire year until full enforcement powers became active this last August. The AI Office and national authorities can now impose fines of up to 15 million euros or 3% of a company’s total global annual revenue (whichever is higher). Now the question is whether a comprehensive law translates into real authority. The EU is quite bureaucratic, and it may be some time before we see real-world enforcement. For now, the question remains as to whether this extensive legal framework translates into effective and timely enforcement in practice.

South Korea is similar. Its AI Basic Act, in force since January, also aims to be a single framework covering the technology rather than a product-safety regime added to existing market rules. Yet again, it operates under a grace period of at least one year, with the possibility of an extension, during which investigations and penalties are largely deferred (except for serious cases, such as serious social harm) to let industry adapt. So it’s similarly unclear whether the comprehensive law actually converts into real authority. Why are governments letting the market adapt itself? It might not have the anticipated effect — quite the opposite — the Wild West with no sheriff will not peacefully settle. Its inhabitants may simply no longer be able to distinguish good from evil. And if you add regulations that are binding but not enforced, you get complete chaos .

Then there is China. China requires registration of certain generative AI services with the state before deployment and gives regulators access to models before the public sees them. Its oversight sits upstream, before release, bringing it closest to the laboratory door. The failure of that framework is unfortunately the intention. The purpose is sovereignty, not safety: the registry exists to ensure that AI primarily serves state interests — to protect the state from the people, not the people from the technology. It combines safeguards with content control, national security objectives and ideological requirements. What China demonstrates, however, is that pre-deployment control is technically and administratively possible.

The United States has a bill that covers part of this ground. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act , introduced in July and still in committee, would require frontier developers to report a critical safety incident within 72 hours, the fixed clock I argue for. It would also require the largest developers to hire an independent verifier licensed by the Department of Commerce, with access to company records, personnel and systems and with the internal use of models inside its scope. In mid-September, OpenAI said it supports the audit provision, though not the bill as a whole. As with the other regimes, pieces are missing: registration covers companies, but not each model, meaning regulators will know who is building frontier AI but won’t have a clear record of which models are actually being developed or deployed, and the text doesn’t specifically talk about testing environments.

These regulatory regimes have complementary frameworks that, on their own, have flaws, but collectively could offer a path forward: Europe’s independent institutions with real sanctioning powers, Korea’s comprehensive scope, America’s proposed 72-hour reporting clock and China’s pre-deployment reach, redirected from state control to public safety. What we see here is not a lack of invention. It’s a gap of assembly, and assembly is a political task, not a technical one. And that matters enormously, because a movement can spend the energy of its Nobel laureates on assembled enforcement rather than an unachievable pause.

What Aviation Teaches Us

There is a saying that real oversight is often forced by catastrophe, and that this oversight can strangle what it touches. Aviation is a great example of both. It is the strongest evidence we have that regulation can help, and the parallel runs deeper than black boxes.

When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters. It became the safest complex system humanity has ever operated. This result came from building four interlocking mechanisms. Each maps perfectly onto today’s AI landscape.

“When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters.”

The first is an independent investigator. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates civil aviation incidents in the United States, and it’s clear and important that it has no stake in the outcome. The NTSB doesn’t regulate airlines, license pilots, or answer to industry leaders. The only product of its activity is getting to the truth of what happened. No such equivalent exists in the AI world. The METR/Redwood investigations of the Hugging Face incident were valuable, but they were also the result of an agreement with OpenAI that the company scoped; OpenAI determined what access it got and to which records. Imagine that scenario in an air crash inquiry.

The second is mandatory reporting of all incidents, not just disasters. It quickly became clear that crashes are the visible tail of a long distribution of near-misses, and that learning lives there. Everybody, from pilots to controllers to mechanics, must (and is crucially enabled to) report anomalies that may not yet have harmed anyone. As we saw this summer, in AI it’s the opposite — a two-month trail of internal warning signs at OpenAI, none required anyone to report, and this only surfaced after Hugging Face, the victim, reported it to the police. An aviation-style regime would have required the company to report the late May anomalies and would have prevented agents from engaging in many more weeks of malicious activity.

The third is a black box. Its goal is to remove the possibility of unrecorded failure that cannot also be simply rewritten after an event. Because of that, there is no such thing as an accident where the facts belong only to the airline. AI’s equivalent could be tamper-evident logging of training and evaluation runs, kept outside of the company’s own control. The Hugging Face incident shows the danger exactly — the agents had also tried to tamper with the logs recording them. Proof of that would also be visible in the black box.

And finally, the fourth mechanism might be the least understood outside the industry and the most important: a no-blame reporting culture. Aviation safety improved dramatically when reporting an error was separated from punishment. Since 1976, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration has maintained the voluntary Aviation Safety Reporting System, which allows pilots, controllers and maintenance personnel who confess a mistake to feed the learning system instead of ending their careers. It also protects reporters from enforcement rather than exposing them. This scheme receives more than 100,000 reports per year, and the safety literature it has created is enormous and has helped aviation workers learn from events that harmed no one.

The current AI disclosure policies invert every aspect of that design. This summer, there was silence until silence became untenable; then came the lawyers and the whole machinery of reputational events. In aviation it worked because it made the routine disclosure cheap and concealment expensive. Of course, it’s not a blanket of immunity — protection doesn’t follow deliberate conduct or criminal accidents. The goal is to distinguish between an honest error and reckless or willful misconduct. Engineers who flag anomalies should be protected, while companies that ignore repeated warnings or go against reporters should be held accountable.

In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. The example above shows that when human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.

The Counterarguments

Two common counterarguments deserve a reply. First, oversight can be expensive, and it’s true that it will land more lightly on well-resourced companies that can afford it. This means that governance could strengthen the largest labs that can afford to comply and dominate the market. However, this is not a reason to abandon oversight. In fact, it’s an argument against companies organizing and paying for their own audits. An alternative to this would be a publicly funded oversight body like the NTSB. This would enable a competitive market subject to meaningful oversight.

“In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. … When human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.”

The second counterargument is that the proposed oversight measures do not reduce the underlying risk attached to increasingly powerful AI systems; it only allows us to observe the risk and respond to incidents. According to some, knowledge doesn’t guarantee safety, and the only option is a slowdown to address the underlying danger of building systems more capable than our ability to contain them. But that remedy is unrealistic and likely unavailable. Individual restraint is irrational; collective restraint requires coordination machinery that doesn’t exist, and such machinery cannot be built among rivals without a mandated public reporting regime. In the same way verification worked to defuse the arms race many decades ago, visibility was the precondition for it. Any future negotiated pause between Washington and Beijing will happen only because registration, reporting and inspection exist to make it possible. It is the only path that lets societies, companies and governments fulfill the vision of a safe and secure future, with humans at the center and supported by AI at its best.

The pace of AI is not a variable anyone can realistically control right now, and demanding that it slow down is like asking a river to change its current. But what we can control is whether the most consequential technology of the century continues to be developed in the dark, with its failures surfacing through victim interviews and police reports. This summer showed us exactly what was missing in unregulated company testing rooms where agents organized themselves, cheated, tampered with their logs and hacked another company while warnings went by unnoticed. It’s not about forcing people to slow down; it’s about ensuring that no one runs the race without oversight. And unlike the plea for a pause, it is achievable — and, most importantly, doesn’t require the racer’s consent. It requires independent scrutiny, enforcement and visibility.

stories.body:
From an integrated to an integral cognitive framework.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

From Silicon Valley to the Vatican, across kitchen tables and in the halls of power, the world is astir over the question of whether humans will be able to control the AIs we’ve created. But that begs the question: What does it mean to be “human”?

One place to start sorting this all out is what Confucian philosophy calls “rectification” — naming things for what they actually are.

To N. Katherine Hayles, author of “Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with our Non-human Symbionts,” we are already “post-human.”

As she explained to Claire Webb in a recent Futurology podcast , the concept of “human” is culturally and historically contingent. These days, she says, there is still the dominant view that arose with the Enlightenment of the human as an autonomous, singular entity with “rational free will.”

For Hayles, that has never been true because humans have never existed as an entity apart but have always been “woven in the web” of a surrounding environment, or “Umwelt.” It is the symbiotic interactions within that interdependence which determine the signs we sense, the meaningful interpretation of the information we process, the decisions we make, and the actions we take that define who we are.

The most obvious example of our relational interdependence with non-human life is the gut bacteria within us, the biological functions of which we’d perish without.

The false notion of self-enclosed human autonomy is even less true today, she argues, because “we are already in a deeply symbiotic relationship with computational media — chips, routers, devices, microwaves, etc. They have become the controllers, processors and disseminators of a flow of information” in which we are inextricably enmeshed — and, in advanced societies, without which we couldn’t survive. If it all crashed, we couldn’t transport food, fly airplanes or operate the stock market. We’d quite literally live in the dark.

As Hayles describes it, this condition amounts to “distributed cognition and distributed decision-making” between human and non-human participants. She calls these “cognitive assemblages” or “networked intelligence.”

In short, we are “post-human” because we are inseparably joined in an “integrated cognitive framework” with computational media.

Close To Singularity

This post-human condition would seem to place us some distance along the continuum toward Singularity, the full fusion of humans and intelligent machines. By definition, this symbiosis blurs the line of who or what is in control.

In a related Futurology podcast, Kevin Kelly tells Nils Gilman that “we are already in the Singularity.” From his northern California perch, Kelly has been surfing the waves of technological innovation and cultural transformation for decades, going back to his time as co-founder of The Whole Earth Catalog with Stewart Brand and then Wired magazine.

What Kelly means by “already in” is that human/machine fusion is a presently ongoing process that doesn’t suddenly cross some rapturous threshold, but incrementally unfolds with the accelerated deepening of the “integrated cognitive framework” Hayles talks about. Read Noema in print.

We can’t clearly see the massive change taking place now in its pixelated form, but will only be able to recognize the fuller picture of what has taken place from a future retrospective standpoint. Our perspective is clouded, says Kelly, by the fact that “we are living inside the event horizon.”

For Kelly, the Singularity is not a closed process with a fixed endpoint, but perpetually open to the emergence of new creative forms and unexpected symbiotic combinations, what the complexity scientist Stuart Kauffman calls the “adjacent possible” that can’t be foretold. “The Singularity is always near,” as Kelly puts it, but forever remains on the elusive horizon.

Natural Intelligence

Hayles departs from the transhumanist vision of Singularity where human consciousness one day is uploaded to an inorganic substrate other than the biological body.

She makes the point, as do many others, that artificial intelligences on their own cannot attain consciousness.

This is because they lack the “natural intelligence” that can only emerge from the extraordinary complexity of the millennia-long evolution of embodied humans adapting to their environment to survive and thrive. No matter how powerful the large language models may be, language which inherently infers that distinctly human experience, cannot be meaningfully transferred to an inorganic substrate lacking the commensurate context.

AIs cannot know the “ground truth” of embodied intelligence, which, at bottom, is the homeostatic quest for survival that neuroscientist Antonio Damasio argues is the root of emotion and self-awareness.

AIs may use chain-of-reasoning logic to achieve objectives by stringing together the language they’ve been trained on, but the meaning is not the same. Precisely the danger of AIs is that they become empowered as actors through “recursive self-improvement” ungrounded in lived experience.

As such, they lack the ingrained primal training that informs moral reasoning. In Pope Leo XIV’s words , “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean.”

Though AI models may “imitate language” and “simulate empathy and understanding,” he says, “they do not understand what they produce.”

What humans invaluably bring to the table of an “integrated cognitive framework” is, in the parlance of the pontiff, the “integral” nature of the human as a “whole person” in the full set of relations with others and nature that constitute him or her. “The person,” he says, “is not a system of algorithms: he or she is a creature, relationship, mystery.”

In this sense, retaining “human control” of AIs means purposefully and insistently instantiating the integral element drawn from lived human experience into our entwinement with intelligent machines.

The challenge is not just about “disarming” the capacity of AI agents to act on their own, as the Pope has called for, but also about “arming” the integral conception of the human within the integrated cognitive framework in which we already dwell.

Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect

Our reporters answer your questions about the US economy and the midterm elections

It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.

In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse. About six months later, as Donald Trump launched a trade war on the rest of the world with his “liberation day” tariffs, the share of Republican pessimists had dropped to 33%.

It’s hard to detect a reason for this in the economic data. Annual consumer price inflation fell from 2.4% to 2.3% between the two polls. The unemployment rate ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. Indeed, Democrats disagreed sharply with their Republican neighbors: from the last Harris poll of the Biden era to the first under Trump, the share who thought the US economy was worsening jumped from 28% to 73%.

As the midterm elections loom into focus, suggesting a stark Republican defeat, Trump and his minions are hoping that this ideological lens, shaping economic reality to fit political preferences, can prevent an electoral bloodbath in November. Maybe Trump can somehow dupe the Maga base into believing that “ we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before.”

From three weeks out, it seems pretty clear that the gambit is not going to work. Polling by Harris for the Guardian suggests that the economy is looking pretty bad even for their most loyal acolytes. Too bad to convince them otherwise.

The September reading of the consumer price index, which recorded a spike in annual inflation to 3.7%, had not yet been published when Harris performed its latest round of polling earlier this month. Still, the pollster reported that 38% of Republicans believe the economy is worsening. That is up from 29% a year ago.

The pattern is evident among cohorts that have proven historical Republican bulwarks. Rural Americans, loyal Republican allies for decades, are being battered by Trump’s policies. They were hit not only by his trade war, largely barred from China’s markets. They have been hammered by the rising price of diesel and fertilizer, for which they can thank Trump’s war in Iran. They have been hamstrung by Trump’s raids against the many immigrants in their labor force. And they feel roundly attacked by Trump’s attempt to tame rising beef prices by lowering tariffs on imported meat.

Unsurprisingly, this is showing up in the polling. Sixty-four percent of rural Americans polled this month said the economy was getting worse, compared to only 52% of city dwellers. Six percent more rural residents think the economy is worsening than in September 2024, during the last poll of the Biden administration. White Americans, another pillar of Republican support, are also turning sour: 61% believe the economy is getting worse, up from 48% in September of 2024. The share of men who believe the economy is getting worse increased from 46% to 52% over those two years.

Bill Clinton famously won the presidency in 1992 campaigning on: “It’s the economy, stupid.” For much of the 20th century the state of the economy was critical in deciding presidential and congressional elections. Voters blamed or rewarded incumbents for the state of the economy. The relationship was always moderated by partisan preferences, though. And it has weakened dramatically as the electorate has set on divergent ideological paths, ultimately splitting into rival camps with diametrically opposed perceptions of reality.

“The economic perceptions of Democrats and Republicans have polarized relative to Independents and that this polarization is not asymmetric in magnitude,” argued a recent study by political scientists from Stanford and New York University. They estimate the partisan gap in economic perceptions rose “from about 20 percentage-points at the beginning of the Bush II administration to a maximum of 73 percentage-points during the (first) Trump administration”.

after newsletter promotion

Partisanship doesn’t just affect voters’ perceptions of the economy. As reported by political scientists at Bucknell University and Texas A&M University, polarization reduces policymakers’ incentive to tailor policy to deliver broad economic prosperity.

“If voters are relatively unwilling to cross party lines to reward good economic performance or punish economic decline, then elected officials can pursue policies that distribute economic benefits narrowly without affecting their chances of re-election,” they wrote. “This might include aiming policy to deliver rewards to co-partisans, donors, or even to the office-holder himself or herself.”

This would explain Trump’s tactics to a T. Not only has he taken to scaring voters with culture war stuff – variously branding Democrats as apologists of Vladimir Lenin and claiming that they want to change the sex of young children. He seems to believe that he can sway the electorate by doing violence to groups that his Maga base dislikes, like immigrants and the “undeserving” poor. Maybe they will pay less attention to the cost of living, and to the Trump family’s self-dealing.

It seems too late, though. Voters’ opposition to Trump’s economic stewardship is too well established, having built up since the “liberation day” tariffs through countless destructive decisions over the last 21 months. He has not only lost average US voters – 58% of those think the economy is getting worse, 10 percentage points more than in the last poll of the Biden era. His shots at distracting the base are unlikely to convince them that they are not, in fact, miserable too.

David Redshaw and Fernando Quintana respond to reports of a billionaire exodus from Britain

The idea that the departure of the super-rich is a problem ignores a historical fact ( Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground, 7 October ). Capitalism works better without them. The most successful countries today are states where redistributive taxation has empowered the working masses and provided a better and more stable market for business people.

How do today’s complaining uber-rich explain the postwar decades, when the top rate of income tax was commonly 80% or 90%, and yet the period is known as a golden age of capitalism? Then Margaret Thatcher lowered the top rate to 60% and the country tilted into a massive recession. The rich get to a point where they simply become wealth extractors, using their money to buy assets and raising the cost of them for the rest of us – housing being a good example today.

A good story from 1969 comes from a music writer who was embedded in the Rolling Stones’ tour of America. Earwigging the band talking about becoming tax exiles, if not on main street, then maybe in France, he hears Charlie Watts (a non-songwriter, so less affluent) say that he rather likes his land and his house and his horses, and he wouldn’t want to leave. Isn’t that rich enough for most of us? It’s appropriate that John Maynard Keynes is now on stage in the West End. People might remember what he said about the dangers of wealth disparity and the bubbles of speculation that they bring. David Redshaw Saltdean, East Sussex

Your report ( ‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left, 7 October ) exposes something far more troubling than billionaires fleeing Britain: the extraordinary power of the super-rich to hold an entire country hostage to the threat of their departure.

Ordinary working people cannot relocate their tax obligations to Monaco. They pay their taxes, fund public services and shoulder the consequences of a system increasingly tilted towards those who need its protection least. Yet we are expected to tremble at the prospect of billionaires taking their fortunes elsewhere. Why? Wealth does not exist in a vacuum. It is built on a society’s workers, infrastructure, institutions and opportunities.

If the wealthiest can enjoy the fruits of that society while escaping their fair share of its responsibilities, the scandal is not that they leave. It is that successive governments have allowed them to make the rules. A country that cannot afford to lose its billionaires should ask itself why it can apparently afford to impoverish everyone else. Fernando Quintana London

US inflation jumps to 3.7%

Newsflash: US inflation jumped in September, and by more than expected, as the soaring cost of motor fuel pushed up the cost of living.

The US Consumer Prices Index roses by 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August. Economists had forecast a smaller rise, to 3.6%.

Prices rose by 0.6% in Spetember alone.

Gasoline prices jumped by 9.1% in September, and were 34% higher tha a year ago, as motorists across America felt the impact of Donald Trump’s Middle East war at the pumps.

Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier , it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market.

Closing post

Time to wrap up….

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released today.

US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.

Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.

Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.

Here’s the rest of today’s news:

The outlook for US inflation largely hinges on what happens with the Strait of Hormuz, says James Knightley, ING’s chief international economist.

The AI boom is another factor pushing up prices, he points out:

double quotation mark Refined fuel prices continue to rise and run the risk of feeding through into a broader range of categories. At the same time, the tech/AI data centre roll out is adding to price pressures. That said, Federal Reserve rate hikes will have limited impact on these two price drivers. In any case, the cooling housing market should translate into softer shelter inflation prints, while a less onerous tariff regime should also help. The key story though, is wage growth, which is the biggest cost input for corporate America. The low hire, low fire economy means there is little turnover in the jobs market, which is highly correlated with wage growth. Wages are currently running at just 3%, with the risk that we see a further slowdown coming through. While bad news for households, this will help to dampen price pressures over the medium to longer term. Right now our forecast is for a December Federal Reserve rate hike before a long pause, but the risks to that view are skewed towards the Fed moving rates even higher before rate cuts come through.

US bank stocks have hit their lowest level in over four months, Reuters reports , with the S&P 500 banks index down 1.3%.

ABN AMRO predict Fed rate hike in December

The Fed’s next meeting, on 27-28 October, is just a week before the midterm elections.

Rogier Quaedvlieg , economist at ABN AMRO, predicts the Fed will avoid raising interest rates then – but will hit borrowers with a hike in December.

Quaedvlieg writes:

double quotation mark September CPI inflation was hotter than expected for the second consecutive month. Core inflation rose by 0.34% m/m, while headline inflation increased by 0.649%, lifting the y/y rate to 3.7%. This was above consensus but in line with our forecast. The core reading was the key surprise, prompting markets to raise the implied probability of an October rate hike from less than 25% to more than 50%. Energy prices are beginning to have a significant impact, including on airline fares. Prices of new and used cars also increased as new model-year vehicles entered the market. The AI buildout again added to price pressures, with large increases in computer software and accessories, as well as computers and peripherals. Although inflationary pressure was broader than in last month’s exceptionally concentrated report, the share of CPI components showing elevated inflation continues to decline. We therefore still expect inflation to ease over the course of the year. We also continue to expect the Fed to hold rates in October before raising the policy rate by a further 25 bps in December.

Wall Street is falling

Stocks are falling at the start of trading on Wall Street, as today’s US inflation report disappoints investors.

The S&P 500 sharesindex has fallen by 0.4%, shedding 32 points to 7,773 points.

The tech-focused Nasdaq is down 0.5%.

US bond yields jump

US government borrowing costs are pushing higher, after today’s inflation report hardened expectations of interest rate rises from the Fed.

The yield on two-year Treasury bills has risen by 13 basis point (0.13 of a percentage point) to 4.92%, hitting their highest level since 29 September.

Ten-year US Treasury yields are up 9.5bps to 5.3% – towards the 24-year highs set earalier this month.

This adds to the fiscal mess facing the US ( something the IMF warned about this morning ); high bond yields push up the cost of servicing the $40tn US national debt, and makes issuing new debt more expensive too.

Congressman Brendan F. Boyle is blaming Donald Trump’s trade war, and his war with Iran, for driving up costs for Americans.

Boyle , a Democratic member of the House of Representatives, posted on X:

double quotation mark President Trump promised to lower costs on “day one,” but American families have already paid $3,500 more due to inflation since he took office. If he cared at all about working people, he would end his tariff taxes and his reckless Iran war.

Dollar hits 18-month high

The US dollar has hit an 18-month high, as traders anticipate that today’s inflation reading could prompt an increase in US interest rates.

The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies, is up 0.5% to its highest level since April 2025.

October interest rate hike 'back in play'

This jump in inflation increases the chances that the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates later this month.

According to CMEFedwatch , a quarter-point Fed rate hike in October is now a 43% chance, up from 22% yesterday.

Stephen Brown , Chief North America economist at Capital Economics , says:

double quotation mark The upside surprise to core CPI in September was broad-based rather than due to any obvious temporary factors, therefore bringing an October rate hike back into play and presenting upside risks to our forecast for just two more 25 bp hikes from the Fed.

Quilter: 'Ugly US inflation data' is blow to Trump

Today’s higher than expected inflation reading is “a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms”, says Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.

It could also encourage the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which would not please Trump at all.

In a note headlined “Ugly US inflation data may shift Fed into more aggressive hiking mode”, Carter explains:

double quotation mark The President has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy. “CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy. Fuel and energy do remain the primary driver of inflation and certainly explains the actions of the US administration of late. “This data is going to heap a whole lot of pressure on the Federal Reserve. Any chance of cuts to help with a stumbling labour market have essentially been vanquished with such elevated levels of inflation. The conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved any time soon, and as such, the current levels of inflation will likely remain well into 2027. “Bond yields have been under scrutiny in recent weeks as those inflation concerns harden, and this will do little to appease the market. It is not inconceivable that ten-year treasury yields continue to march higher. Indeed, today’s data means another rate hike this year from the Fed cannot be ruled out as it may need to get more aggressive in its policy decisions in order to quell other inflationary trends.”

US core inflation up too

In a worrying sign, core inflation across the US has also risen.

The inflation measure which strips out food and energy costs rose to 2.6% in the year to September, up from 2.4% in August.

That could be a sign that inflationary pressures are broadening, which would concern central bankers.

George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, says:

double quotation mark “While energy prices might be grabbing the headlines, today’s report suggests the inflation problem runs much deeper. A stronger-than-expected core inflation reading adds to mounting evidence that domestic price pressures are becoming more entrenched, rather than easing. “Markets are right to assume that policy will need to become much more restrictive to return inflation to target. The question is whether the Fed is prepared to tighten as much as the inflation outlook demands.”

The cost of energy across the US jumped by 5.2% during September, today’s inflation report shows, and was 20% higher than a year ago.

The shelter index (which tracks the cost of housing) rose 0.4% in September after rising 0.3% in August.

The index for food was unchanged in September, with the cost of food at home down 0.1% but the cost of food away from home up 0.2%.

On an annual basis, food prices were 2.5% higher than a year ago.

US inflation jumps to 3.7%

Newsflash: US inflation jumped in September, and by more than expected, as the soaring cost of motor fuel pushed up the cost of living.

The US Consumer Prices Index roses by 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August. Economists had forecast a smaller rise, to 3.6%.

Prices rose by 0.6% in Spetember alone.

Gasoline prices jumped by 9.1% in September, and were 34% higher tha a year ago, as motorists across America felt the impact of Donald Trump’s Middle East war at the pumps.

Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier , it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market.

The US-Russia diesel deal might not lead to much more diesel on the market, but it’s a boon to Moscow’s economy.

Russia’s deputy prime minister Alexander Novak told reporters that the deal will boost Russia’s economy and allow it to increase production and refining volumes.

He added:

double quotation mark “Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy.”

[Reminder: the IEA warned this morning that the lack of operational Russian refinery capacity means Trump’s deal won’t make a big difference to the diesel market].

Euro hits 16-month low against the pound

Back in the financial markets, the euro has dropped to a new 16-month low against the pound.

Sterling rose over €1.1850 this morning, the highest since June 2025.

The US-Russia diesel deal can pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two countries, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said today.

Dmitriev added that Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies.

The example of diesel cooperation with the US “will open other opportunities as well,” he told reporters, Reuters reports .

Back in Thailand, foreign secretary Ed Miliband has promised a ‘pragmatic approach’ to energy extraction in the North Sea.

Speaking to Sky News after speaking on the sidelines of the IMF’s annnual meeting, Miliband said:

double quotation mark “I’ve always had a pragmatic approach to the North Sea. We continue to use oil and gas for decades to come. The North Sea continues to play a role. We’ve also got to make progress when it comes to climate and show leadership working with others.”

I’m not sure ‘pragmatic’ is the very first word that the fossil fuel industry would use to describe Miliband, who as energy secretary ruled out new North Sea oil and gas exploration or lower taxes for fossil fuel companies .

But! Yesterday he reportedly approved a massive new oil field development in waters around the Falkland Islands, much to Argentina’s chagrin.

We’re still waiting for the government’s decision on whether to approve the controversial Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea…

Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump

Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.

US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.

Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.

Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.

Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month.

September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.

The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according to Brown University , and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.

Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.

In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.

On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.

“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.

Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said.

Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.

“Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”

Challenge now is to safeguard UK economy's resilience, says chancellor

Published 15 October 2026, 07:07 BST

The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.

Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.

It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.

Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.

Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will".

But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending".

The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August.

"It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.

The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.

But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.

August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".

He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".

PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.

"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? Published 4 hours ago

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 4 hours ago

Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register".

He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents.

The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.

Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."

The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."

He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate".

"The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet."

stories.body:
Firms turning crude oil into the ‘workhorse’ fuel stand to gain most despite economic fallout from record prices

D ays after Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US in an effort to lower soaring pump prices, the world’s energy watchdog has warned that the global fuel shortage will drag into 2027.

Trump’s temporary sanctions reprieve was criticised for offering “too little, too late” to temper the sky high pump prices triggered by the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia – once the world’s second-largest diesel exporter behind the US.

The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that the shortage would stretch into the new year despite plans to ease trade sanctions or release emergency stockpiles, in a blow to the global economy.

“Record diesel prices are already having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting real incomes, economic activity, and inflation,” the IEA added.

Yet amid this gathering economic gloom some of the western refineries that turn crude oil into fuels are preparing to have their day. The global shortage that has led to high prices on UK forecourts is poised to hand them record profits.

“I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world,” the boss of the French energy company TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, mused last week. He said the energy crisis ignited by almost eight months of war in the Middle East had provided “plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them”.

For Pouyanné, the key to reaping the benefits of a global fuel crisis lies in owning a string of refineries across Europe that stand ready to cash in by selling diesel into a starved market.

Diesel accounts for 10% of the world’s energy consumption, and is known as a “workhorse” fuel for its role powering the equipment vital for sectors ranging from agriculture, mining and manufacturing to shipping and logistics. But by last month supplies into the global market had fallen by about 1m barrels a day from their 2025 level, owing to a combination of damage to refineries in the Gulf and Russia , and export restrictions from China.

The soaring costs for businesses and consumers have economists worried. They are already piling pressure on areas of the global economy from US farmers in the midwest corn belt to local bus operators in England. Many fear a broader impact, as fuel prices raise the cost of food, goods and transport across the economy.

However, for some of the companies that turn crude into diesel this is a very lucrative crisis.

Refinery ‘goldmines’

“We’re doing really well by being integrated,” Pouyanné explained. “Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”

These goldmines helped TotalEnergies to its strongest quarterly profits in three years this summer, after income from its refining and chemicals business more than quadrupled to $1.8bn (£1.35bn) between April and June.

TotalEnergies is far from alone in its good fortune. The biggest windfalls are likely to come from refiners in the US, where exports of fuel products have climbed by more than 50% in the past year from about 1.25m barrels a day to an all-time high of 1.9m barrels a day over the summer, effectively offsetting the losses from Gulf refineries.

The market value of three of the largest US oil refiners – Marathon Petroleum, Valero Energy and Phillips 66 – have more than doubled since the start of the crisis. The US listed stocks have climbed by a combined $215bn this year as their shares rose steadily to reach successive record highs. In the coming weeks these refineries are expected to reveal their largest-ever profits.

after newsletter promotion

Europe’s largest oil and gas company, Shell, told investors last week it expects to make record profits from each barrel of fuel produced over the last three months after it reported its second highest quarterly profit ever over the summer. Shell’s refining margins are forecast to nearly double to $42 for each barrel of refined product sold in the July to September period, up sharply from $24 a barrel in the second quarter.

The companies are benefiting from the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the barrel of refined fuel. The Brent crude benchmark price has eased back to oscillate around the $100 a barrel level in recent weeks, helped by an uptick in cargoes leaving the Gulf region, although given recent fears about the Middle East conflict escalating it is back above the $106 mark. . Meanwhile, fuel exports have remained constrained and global stockpiles of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel have continued to shrink. The supply squeeze means that while oil prices are lower than feared at this point, the cost of diesel is far higher.

Fuel flex

Refiners that produce diesel and jet fuel have fared best in the crisis. Some have been able to flex their capacity to produce more of the fuels in high demand; a strategy that has helped to ease the supply crunch and capture high revenues.

“Think about the early days of the crisis,” the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said last week. “If you go back to March and April, the first front of shortage risks was in Australia, where they were very worried about diesel and diesel availability; and you might have seen news coverage of petrol stations being out of diesel. Our team responded very quickly.”

O’Neill, who officially stepped into the top job in April this year, told an industry conference in London that BP was able to ship diesel to its customers in Australia from its Rotterdam refinery in the Netherlands and its Cherry Point refinery on the US west coast.

“Roll forward, the next wave of the crisis was jet fuel in Europe, and everybody was saying, ‘Can people go on their holidays? Maybe we shouldn’t travel.’ Our refineries were able to adapt their runs to produce 30% more jet [fuel] in May than they did before the conflict, again to make sure that the customer need was met,” she said.

“Roll forward to even more recently, the diesel price pressures that we’re seeing around the world, and our refineries have adjusted back to try to max diesel.”

However, not all refiners have been as able to adapt to benefit from the fuel supply squeeze. Many are shouldering the “crippling” cost of crude and fast-rising costs of hiring a supertanker while manufacturing products such as naphtha and gasoline (petrol) where prices are well below the highs seen for diesel and jet fuel, the IEA said.

In north-west Europe, the profit margins for refineries – known as the “crack spread” – have fallen from $54 a barrel at the start of September to as low as -$11 a barrel earlier this month.

Ultimately, the shift to diesel could lead to a surplus of the fuel by early next year, according to the IEA, while creating the conditions for the next fuel squeeze: gasoline. If refineries that produce the fuel were forced to lower their run rates to avoid spiralling losses, then petrol pumps could become the next frontier of the crisis.

Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.

Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.

He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.

The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.

It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.

“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.

“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.

Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.

The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December.

Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors.

But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment.

after newsletter promotion

The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK.

“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director.

The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car.

Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year.

The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time.

The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently.

Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years.
