stories.summary: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei

Published 15 October 2026, 02:14 BST

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential.

Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech.

It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI.

Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.

The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs.

Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability.

Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models.

Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down .

In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade , and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity .

The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons .

However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been " bringing up things that won't happen " and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins".

Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns.

The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.

How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections Published 14 hours ago

'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire Published 1 day ago

Market sentiment

Anthropic's revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, are an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.

Stocks in some US technology companies dropped on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.

Shares in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank were down by more than 9% on Thursday. South Korean semiconductor giants also dropped, with Samsung falling by 9.5% and SK Hynix 11% lower.

Shares have been falling this week after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.

Tan said at a conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".

The falls deepened after US inflation data released on Wednesday showed price rises accelerated by more than expected in September.

Investors are concerned that higher inflation will mean the US Federal Reserve is more likely to put up the cost of borrowing.

A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.

ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.

Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.

The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.

The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.

A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”

China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.

The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.

The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.

The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.

The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.

It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.

A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”

The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”

The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.

In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.

He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”

Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.

He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”

Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”

A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”

ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.

One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.

Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”

Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

stories.summary: In an extremely disappointing ruling , a California trial court dismissed SIREN v. San Jose , our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including one issued just months ago . It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country. San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. The court disagreed, explaining that based on one California appeals court case involving individual streetlight cameras, people do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy when driving on a public road. This is wrong. Networked ALPRs are not individual streetlight cameras. Their net effect of tracking and mapping cars as they travel reveals patterns of life, intimate relationships, and much more. Fortunately, there are signs that the tide is turning against ALPRs in the courts. stories.title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
stories.summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.

stories.title: Suarez scores again as Sporting beat Lens
stories.summary: Luis Suarez scores for an eighth consecutive match as he helps Sporting beat Lens 2-0 in France, as the Portuguese side make it two wins from two in this season's Champions League.

stories.title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
stories.summary: District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last month A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out. Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.
